title: From Human Videos to Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Data: Confidence-Guided RL Refinement of Video Priors
summary: Collecting demonstrations for bimanual dexterous manipulation is costly, motivating the use of human videos as a source of robot training data. However, uncertainty in video-derived motion estimates and differences between human and robot embodiments make direct motion transfer challenging. In this work, we introduce PriDex, a framework that transforms human-video Priors into executable robot Dexterous manipulation demonstrations through reinforcement learning in simulation. PriDex preserves task-relevant interaction structure while allowing embodiment-specific behavior to be regenerated for the robot. Human-object interactions provide affordance cues for selecting task-relevant, robot-specific grasps from geometry-based candidates. For motion refinement, object trajectories provide a task-level reference, while relative bimanual wrist trajectories offer complementary guidance for coordinated motion. Since object-motion estimates can become unreliable under occlusion or visual ambiguity, PriDex uses object-motion confidence to adaptively balance these two priors, emphasizing object-level guidance when confidence is high and increasing the contribution of wrist-level guidance as confidence decreases. Reinforcement learning refines these video-derived priors under the robot's kinematic and physical constraints, and the resulting policies are rolled out to generate robot demonstrations for training a vision-based diffusion policy. We evaluate PriDex on four bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks, including pouring, sweeping into a dustpan, bottle-cap unscrewing, and plate cleaning, assessing both simulation-based robot data generation and downstream visuomotor policy learning.

INTRODUCTION Learning bimanual dexterous manipulation requires large amounts of high-quality robot interaction data. Collecting such data directly on robots is particularly demanding for high-dimensional dexterous systems, where demonstrations must coordinate two arms, multiple fingers, and contact-rich object interactions over extended horizons. Human manipulation videos provide an appealing alternative: they are abundant, naturally capture coordinated bimanual behavior, and contain rich cues about where and how objects are manipulated~ hoque2026egodex,Grauman_2022_CVPR . However, these videos do not directly provide supervision that can be readily transferred to robots. Human and robot hands differ substantially in morphology and kinematics, while object and hand motions recovered from video can be inaccurate due to occlusion, partial observability, and reconstruction uncertainty. To extract more actionable supervision from human videos, recent approaches reconstruct 3D hand and object motions and use the resulting trajectories for retargeting, reinforcement learning, or simulation-based skill acquisition~ chen2025vividex,lum2025crossing,dan2025xsim,han2026video2sim2real,paliwal2026doasido,ren2026c2dex . However, reconstructed motions remain only approximate proxies for robot behavior. Their quality can vary due to partial observability and reconstruction uncertainty, while even accurately recovered human motions may not transfer directly to a robot because of differences in kinematics and collision constraints. Consequently, video-derived motion should not be treated as uniformly reliable or directly executable robot supervision. The key challenge is therefore not simply how faithfully to reproduce reconstructed human motion, but which cues from the video should guide robot learning and when. Our key insight is to separate transferable interaction structure from embodiment-specific motion when transferring human demonstrations to robots. Human videos provide useful cues about where interaction occurs and how the manipulated object evolves, whereas exact human grasp configurations and hand motions are strongly embodiment-dependent and therefore need not be reproduced by the target robot. We therefore preserve interaction cues that transfer more naturally across embodiments, while allowing grasping and motion details to be regenerated and refined for the robot. This reframes human-video transfer from reproducing human motion to preserving the interaction structure most relevant to successful execution. Following this principle, we introduce PriDex, a confidence-guided framework that converts human-video priors into executable bimanual dexterous robot demonstrations through reinforcement learning in simulation. PriDex first infers affordance regions from human-object interactions and uses them to sample task-relevant robot grasps from geometry-based candidates~ chen2025dexonomy,chen2025bodex , avoiding direct retargeting of human grasp configurations that may be sensitive to pose-estimation uncertainty and embodiment differences. For motion learning, object trajectories provide the primary reference for the desired evolution of the manipulated object. Since the reliability of object-motion estimates can vary over time, PriDex complements this object-level reference with wrist-motion cues that capture how each hand moves from the onset of interaction. These wrist trajectories provide a coarser motion cue that is less dependent on detailed hand morphology. PriDex then uses object-motion confidence to adaptively balance the two guidance signals, emphasizing object-level supervision when confidence is high and placing greater weight on wrist-level guidance as confidence decreases. Reinforcement learning refines these video-derived priors under the robot's kinematic and physical constraints, producing coordinated behaviors without requiring exact reproduction of the demonstrated human motion. Finally, the learned policies are rolled out in simulation to generate bimanual dexterous robot demonstrations, which are subsequently distilled into a vision-based diffusion policy~ chi2023diffusionpolicy for downstream visuomotor control. We evaluate PriDex on four bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks from the EgoDex dataset~ hoque2026egodex , including sweeping, pouring, bottle-cap unscrewing, and plate cleaning. Starting from only three human videos per task, PriDex performs reinforcement learning in Isaac Sim~ nvidiaisaacsim to expand these demonstrations into hundreds of robot trajectories for downstream policy learning. We evaluate the resulting data-generation pipeline through simulation RL and downstream visuomotor policy learning, examining both skill acquisition and the utility of the generated demonstrations. In summary, our contributions are as follows: We introduce a human-video-to-robot framework that converts video-derived priors into executable bimanual dexterous robot demonstrations through reinforcement learning in simulation, allowing robot behavior to be refined beyond direct human-motion retargeting. We develop a structured prior refinement strategy that preserves transferable interaction cues while adapting embodiment-specific behavior, combining affordance-aware grasp selection with confidence-guided motion refinement. We evaluate PriDex on four bimanual dexterous tasks from EgoDex, generating thousands of robot trajectories from only 12 human manipulation videos for simulation and downstream visuomotor policy learning. Related Work Learning Robot Manipulation from Human Videos Human videos provide a scalable source of manipulation supervision without requiring extensive robot demonstrations. Early approaches mainly use them as high-level or embodiment-agnostic guidance. MimicPlay~ wang2023mimicplay learns latent plans from human play to guide low-level policies trained with robot demonstrations, while Im2Flow2Act~ xu2025flow uses 2D object flow as a cross-embodiment interface between human videos and simulated robot experience. More recent methods recover explicit 3D motion to provide denser supervision. X-Sim~ dan2025xsim uses object trajectories extracted from RGB-D demonstrations to guide gripper-based manipulation, whereas DexMV~ qin2022dexmv , ViViDex~ chen2025vividex , and DemoBot~ xu2026demobot rely on retargeting reconstructed human hand motion to dexterous robot hands. Recent work has begun to reduce reliance on full hand-motion imitation. Human2Sim2Robot~ lum2025crossing uses human hand poses primarily to initialize manipulation and object trajectories as task-level guidance, while DexImit~ mu2026deximit synthesizes feasible robot motion from reconstructed human demonstrations rather than directly replaying human hand trajectories. These methods progressively move beyond direct human-motion retargeting toward more selective use of video-derived supervision. PriDex instead transfers video-derived cues according to their cross-embodiment transferability and dynamically balances complementary motion priors during RL-based exploration and refinement. Dexterous Manipulation Dexterous manipulation remains challenging due to its high-dimensional action space and contact-rich dynamics, making demonstration collection considerably more demanding than for parallel-gripper manipulation. Existing systems acquire dexterous supervision through instrumented human-motion capture systems~ wang2024dexcap , direct robot teleoperation~ qin2023anyteleop , or human-to-robot motion retargeting~ qin2022dexmv . The challenge becomes more pronounced for bimanual dexterous manipulation, which requires coordinated control of two arms and multi-fingered hands. To improve data scalability, DexMimicGen~ jiang2025dexmimicgen expands a small set of source teleoperated demonstrations into large bimanual datasets through automated simulation generation. ManipTrans~ li2025maniptrans pre-trains a dexterous policy on large-scale human hand trajectories and subsequently learns task-specific residual actions for interaction-aware refinement. These approaches progressively reduce the cost of dexterous data acquisition, but still rely on costly instrumented human motion-capture systems or teleoperated robot demonstrations. PriDex instead extracts task-relevant priors from monocular human videos and uses them to generate physically executable bimanual dexterous robot rollouts through reinforcement learning. Method Problem Formulation and Overview sec:overview Given a human manipulation video and the associated camera calibration, our goal is to generate bimanual dexterous robot demonstrations that preserve the task-relevant interaction in the video while adapting its realization to the robot's embodiment and physical constraints. Rather than treating reconstructed human motion as directly executable supervision, PriDex recovers structured interaction priors from the video to guide robot behavior in simulation. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:pipeline , PriDex first extracts object and bimanual wrist trajectories, together with time-varying object-motion confidence (Sec.~ sec:priors ). Contact-derived affordance cues guide the selection of task-relevant robot grasps from geometry-based candidates, avoiding direct transfer of human grasp configurations (Sec.~ sec:grasp_init ). These grasps initialize confidence-guided RL, with object trajectories providing task-level references and relative wrist motion offering complementary coordination guidance (Sec.~ sec:rl_refinement ). Confidence modulates these priors while RL adapts motion to robot kinematics and contact dynamics. Finally, successful simulation rollouts train a vision-based Diffusion Policy~ chi2023diffusionpolicy for downstream visuomotor control (Sec.~ sec:policy_distillation ). title: DreamFAR: Real-Time and Long-Horizon Interaction with Diverse Objects
summary: World models have shown great potential in serving as a simulator for robot manipulation. However, existing models are either fit to a single environment or lack ability to simulate long-horizon contact-rich events. We present DreamFAR, a world model whose dynamics model is trained from scratch on a large robot-native teleoperation dataset, with no internet-video pretraining. We present an architecture and learning recipe designed for training on robot-native data. DreamFAR is significantly smaller than the high-performance video generation models, yet shows better understanding of contact and causality, and runs 10 FPS on a commercial GPU. Experimentally, DreamFAR significantly outperforms existing models in predicting the long-horizon future. We further demonstrate various applications where DreamFAR can be used, including policy evaluation and mixed-data co-training. Project page: https://www.yimingdou.com/DreamFAR/

Project page: www.yimingdou.com/DreamFAR Introduction sec:intro A world model~ ha2018world predicts the future conditioned on an action input. The major appeal of learning such model is that it's a powerful abstraction of the world for dynamics and control, allowing robots to plan many steps into the future, simulate the outcomes of their behavior and like humans~ flanagan1997role , search for the optimal actions in order to achieve their goals. Given these strengths, what prevents world models from being the prominent tool for solving contact-rich manipulation tasks? One of the major shortcomings of today's world models is their inability to do long-horizon prediction ~ gao2026dreamdojo,ye2026dreamzero,ali2025cosmospredict . Rolling out future predictions for long horizons, even for tens of seconds, often leads to catastrophic error accumulation. And even when some world models do achieve long-horizon prediction ~ wang2026interactive , they often struggle with generalization , as they are unable to properly model the physics of the diverse contact-rich manipulation scenarios that robots commonly interact with. We propose , a world model for real-time, long-horizon, contact-rich interaction across diverse objects and scenes. Our key contribution is a contact-based memory context, motivated by the need to remember how earlier interactions changed the scene even after objects left view. We combine a short window of recent frames with a set of long-term keyframes, capturing ongoing motion and past interactions without expanding the attention context. Inspired by human haptic memory hutmacher2018long , we select keyframes at contact-making or breaking moments, when robot--object interactions change the scene structure. The model predicts these events to update its memory during rollouts without external contact annotations, and retrieves keyframes by end-effector-pose similarity to recall relevant object states. Together with other architectual choices decisions detailed in the method section, we demonstrate that generalizes to diverse scenes and tasks, sustains minutes of open-loop rollouts under recorded actions, and supports live teleoperation at 10 \,Hz. Compared with state-of-the-art world models trained on the same robot dataset, DreamFAR produces more accurate predictions and accumulates less visual error over long rollouts. We evaluate this on 1,000 held-out scenes, where it achieves higher average prediction quality over one-minute rollouts (Fig.~ fig:drift ). We also evaluate by the correlation between policy rollouts inside our model and the real world: across two policy checkpoints and three tasks, simulated and real-robot mean task progress have a Pearson correlation of (Fig.~ fig:poleval ). Finally, we demonstrate that data collected inside the simulator can improve real-robot policy performance. Experimentally, training a policy on mixed real-world and simulator demonstrations increases the task progress by two-fold compared to a policy trained on real-world demonstrations alone. Related Work sec:related Video-generator world models. Most recent robot world models pretrain a large video generator on internet-scale videos, followed by post-training on robot specific data agarwal2025cosmos,ali2025cosmospredict,guo2025ctrl,ye2026dreamzero,gao2026dreamdojo . These models typically contain billions of parameters, ranging from 2B to 14B agarwal2025cosmos,ali2025cosmospredict . While large-scale video pretraining provides useful physical priors, accurately reproducing physical dynamics remains challenging kang2024physical,motamed2025physics , and extending generation beyond the training horizon can lead to accumulating errors song2025history,zhang2025framepack . takes the opposite route: its dynamics are trained causally from scratch on robot-native data and stream frame by frame. Causal world models on robot or agent data. A parallel line of work train on robot-specific data from the start. Termed by ha2018world , World Models jointly learn action-conditioned future observation prediction by factorizing the problem into representation learning (mapping high dimensional observations into latent state vectors), dynamics prediction (future state prediction conditioned on current state and actions) and future image generation (mapping a low dimensional future state into a high dimensional observation). Follow up works like DREAMER hafner2019learning and many others use this framework for planning, RL and control hafner2025training,alonso2024diffusion,bruce2024genie . Model-based RL silver2017mastering, deisenroth2011pilco, levine2013guided works predate this recent interest in world modeling. On robots, action-conditioned video prediction from robot-only data dates to finn2016unsupervised and continues with autoregressive, diffusion and feature-space predictors wu2024ivideogpt,zhu2024irasim,zhou2024dino,li2026causal . Closest to ours are WEAVER jain2026weaver , a causal world model trained on robot-native manipulation data, and the Interactive World Simulator (IWS) wang2026interactive , which adds real-time, long-horizon interactive generation. Long-horizon and memory mechanisms. Two fundamental mechanisms allow modern video generators to model worlds; first, generation which controls how errors compound, e.g., per-frame noise levels, KV-cached or rolling-window denoising, training on the model's own rollouts chen2024diffusion,yin2024slow,huang2026self,liu2025rolling , and a frame-level attention sink on the initial generated frame(s) yang2025longlive,liu2025rolling . Second, conditioning which decides what to remember: compressed history, frame banks retrieved by camera pose or field-of-view overlap, or explicit 3D maps zhang2025framepack,xiao2025worldmem,yu2025context,wu2025video ; on robots, Ctrl-World and WEAVER keep pose-conditioned time-strided history frames guo2025ctrl,jain2026weaver . adapts both to manipulation: the per-frame noise levels become a streaming pyramid of in-flight frames served from a rolling KV cache, the sink is one learned, never-noised, never-evicted frame, and memory keeps pose-similarity retrieval but changes what is eligible: keyframes are recorded when the contact transitions the model itself predicts (Sec.~ method:memory ) happen. Policy evaluation and data generation. Physics simulators with real-to-sim assets rank policies in agreement with real trials li2024evaluating,zhang2025real,badithela2025reliable, jain2025polaris , but each scene is built by hand. Learned world models skip the assets: policies are rolled out and scored inside the model quevedo2025worldgym,li2025worldeval,tseng2026sc3 or trained on generated data jang2025dreamgen , and IWS reports real-to-simulated correlation of policy outcomes wang2026interactive . targets the same two uses as a streaming simulator in which a policy, or a human through leader arms, acts closed-loop at 10\,Hz. Method sec:method Let and denote the visual observation and robot action at time , and their history. We learn an action-conditioned world model that generates future observations autoregressively: During rollout, incorporates the model's own predictions, enabling long-horizon simulation driven by recorded actions, a policy, or a human operator. To achieve this goal, we propose , a latent flow-matching model that combines a visual tokenizer to encode observations into a compact latent space with a dynamics transformer to predict action-conditioned state transitions. We describe how unit-sphere normalization constrains latent scale (Sec.~ method:tokenizer ), how predicted contact transitions and pose-based retrieval select long-term memories to complement recent context (Sec.~ method:memory ), and how hybrid attention, pipelined denoising over a rolling KV cache, and a persistent attention sink enable streaming prediction (Sec.~ method:dynamics ). Contact-Based Memory method:memory A short context window can forget earlier interactions, such as where an object was placed after it leaves view. We therefore represent the visual history in using both a window of recent latents and a long-term memory set . The recent window captures ongoing motion, while memory retains selected earlier observations without expanding the transformer's context with rollout length. We select memory keyframes based on predicted contact transitions, which mark the onset or end of robot--object interactions. An auxiliary head on the dynamics transformer predicts two contact bits , one per arm; a change in either predicted contact adds the corresponding frame to the keyframe bank. The head is trained with binary cross-entropy loss against label predictions from a fine-tuned vision-language model clark2026molmo2 , with gradients detached from the dynamics backbone. During rollout, the model updates the bank using its own contact predictions, requiring no external contact labels. To construct , we retain an initial anchor frame and retrieve keyframes preceding the recent window, ranked by end-effector-pose similarity to that window and recency. Poses are computed from predicted joint states via forward kinematics. Retrieved frames carry relative time offsets, and unused slots are masked, giving a fixed memory budget of eight frames. Labeling, retrieval, and training details are provided in App.~ app:method . Streaming Dynamics Transformer method:dynamics Our causal dynamics transformer predicts conditioned on action , recent latents , and memory , while jointly predicting the robot's joint state, as well as contact. Hybrid attention combines spatial attention within frames and causal temporal attention across frames, with selected layers using joint spatio-temporal attention to capture motion across spatial positions. A learned sink frame~ xiao2024efficient , never noised or evicted, provides a persistent attention target even when memory slots are empty. We train with latent flow matching and independently sampled noise levels per frame, following diffusion forcing chen2024diffusion . For streaming inference, we maintain frames at staggered flow times and denoise them in parallel using a rolling KV cache liu2026rolling,jain2026weaver . Each model call advances all in-flight frames, commits the oldest to the recent context, evicts the oldest context frame, and admits a new noise frame conditioned on the next action. Caching the committed context, memory, and sink keeps the dynamics computation per step constant in rollout length, while pipelining introduces a delay of steps between an action and its rendered frame. Unit-Sphere Tokenizer method:tokenizer Our tokenizer uses a finetuned SSDD~ vallaeys2026ssdd image encoder to map each observation to a compact latent for dynamics modeling. We apply unit-sphere normalization davidson2018hyperspherical,loshchilov2024ngpt to the encoded tokens and re-normalize predicted tokens before decoding and reuse as context to limit scale drift. A flow-matching decoder reconstructs each camera view conditioned on its latent . title: AR-WAM: efficient streaming world-action modeling for autonomous driving
summary: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.
full_text: \@topnum @ Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines. Introduction sec:introduction End-to-end driving policies increasingly build on pretrained foundation models. Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer semantic knowledge from image-text pretraining to trajectory prediction li2025recogdrive,li2026drivevlaw0 . World-action models (WAMs) instead start from video foundation models, whose pretraining on how scenes evolve provides priors over geometry, motion and near-future dynamics shi2026drivewam,xia2026drivelaw,liu2026driveva,zhao2026simwam . These priors suit driving, because the scene changes continuously and the right action depends on how other road users are moving: a lead vehicle at the same distance may be braking or pulling away, and a single image often cannot tell the two apart. A driving policy therefore needs recent observations, which reveal changes in relative position and speed. Current-image policies, including OpenVLA and in robot manipulation kim2024openvla,black2025pi0 and current-frame driving WAMs zhao2026simwam , omit this visual history, although memory-based policies demonstrate its value on temporally dependent tasks shi2026memoryvla . Driving WAMs such as DriveVA and DriveLaW do encode a window of recent frames liu2026driveva,xia2026drivelaw . With bidirectional temporal attention, however, historical features depend on the other frames in the window, so each new observation requires re-encoding the window yin2025causvid . More history then buys motion information at the cost of computation repeated at each decision. Future prediction adds a second source of latency. WAMs such as DriveWAM and DriveVA iteratively predict future video before or alongside action generation shi2026drivewam,liu2026driveva , so each decision pays for video denoising even when, as in DriveWAM, the observed history is cached. To avoid this cost, Fast-WAM and SimWAM remove future video tokens at inference while retaining video supervision during training yuan2026fastwam,zhao2026simwam . Yet Simple-WAM shows, in controlled comparisons on robot manipulation, that retaining future conditioning improves generalization, and that a single forward pass over fully noised future tokens recovers most of the benefit zhou2026simplewam . Motivated by these findings, we seek a driving policy that uses both temporal history and predictive features without repeating observation encoding or generating future video iteratively. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Because causal attention makes the keys and values (K/V) of completed observation chunks reusable when new frames arrive, as in streaming video generation yin2025causvid,huang2025selfforcing , AR-WAM updates its visual history incrementally and makes it available to future prediction. Autoregressive pretraining also learns how future states depend on past observations, and recent manipulation results show that it can strengthen the benefit of visual history huang2026longwam . We therefore ask how much test-time future prediction contributes once the policy already observes recent motion, and how much of it a driving decision needs. At each decision, AR-WAM computes only what has changed. It adds the new observation to its cache and looks ahead with one backbone pass over the current image and fully noised future tokens. Its trajectory expert then reads the resulting predictive features and the cached history at matching backbone depths, so no future video is denoised. The ego state and driving command also change at every decision, and conditioning the history on them would require recomputing it each time huang2026longwam . AR-WAM therefore applies them only to the predictive pass and the expert, which keeps the cache valid as driving intent changes. We train video and trajectory prediction jointly, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards liu2025flowgrpo,zhao2026simwam . Built on OmniDreams, a pretrained causal video backbone nvidia2026omnidreams , with a single front camera, AR-WAM attains a higher NAVSIM-v1 PDMS than strong WAMs that rely on bidirectional video backbones, such as SimWAM, which plans from a single observation, and UNIVERSE, which re-encodes a window of frames liu2026universe . In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, it also outscores both while running 3.4 and 1.8 times faster, and visual memory accounts for most of its lead over SimWAM. With this history available, one predictive pass matches ten passes of joint future denoising at under a quarter of their latency, and its benefit shows on the perturbed NAVHARD scenes. After refinement with the EPDMS reward, AR-WAM reaches the highest NAVSIM-v2 EPDMS on both NAVTEST and NAVHARD among the compared WAMs that predict a single trajectory without scoring candidates at test time. Our contributions are: We introduce AR-WAM, a causal world-action model that plans from an incrementally updated cache of observed history and a single predictive pass. Two designs keep this cache reusable: the ego state and driving command enter only the per-decision pass, and decision-relative attention lets one trajectory expert read cached and predictive features at any point of a stream. We study the role of test-time future prediction once visual history is available, and integrate it into autoregressive world-action modeling as a single backbone pass over noised future tokens. We demonstrate strong single-camera planning performance, achieving 91.5 NAVSIM-v1 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning. In the dynamic setting, AR-WAM scores higher than the compared world-action models at lower latency. Related work sec:related Future modeling at test time. World-action models are trained to predict the future, but they differ in how much of it they compute when they act. Generating future video before or alongside the trajectory shi2026drivewam,liu2026driveva makes every decision pay for iterative denoising. To avoid this latency, Fast-WAM, SimWAM and UNIVERSE keep video prediction as a training signal and remove the future tokens at inference yuan2026fastwam,zhao2026simwam,liu2026universe . The action head then reads no predictive features, however, and Simple-WAM and Faster-WAM show in manipulation that this costs generalization zhou2026simplewam,zhao2026fasterwam . Other methods keep predictive features while avoiding a full rollout at every decision xia2026drivelaw,zhang2025epona,zhang2026rift,fan2026drivehwm,ang2026adaptivewam , and Simple-WAM finds that a single pass over pure-noise future tokens recovers most of the loss. Yet it and Adaptive-WAM establish this only for policies that see the current observation, so it remains unclear how such a pass should work beside a cache of history and how much it adds once the policy observes recent motion. Building on the single-pass insight, AR-WAM computes predictive features in one pass that attends to cached observation history, and compares it with a variant without future tokens and with full denoising. Visual history and memory. The right action depends on motion that a single image does not show. SimWAM and Adaptive-WAM nevertheless plan from the current frame zhao2026simwam,ang2026adaptivewam , and so cannot observe how other road users are moving. DriveVA, DriveLaW and UNIVERSE observe motion through a window of recent frames liu2026driveva,xia2026drivelaw,liu2026universe , but because the window is encoded again whenever a frame arrives, their cost grows with the history they keep. Caching the K/V of observed frames removes this repetition. DriveWAM caches observed video and action chunks shi2026drivewam , yet it generates future video at every decision, and on NAVSIM it makes a single prediction from the current frame, so its memory plays no role there. In manipulation, Long-WAM reuses the K/V of observed frames within one action solve and notes what would invalidate them across decisions, such as an updated robot state or shifted temporal positions huang2026longwam , whereas MemoryVLA++ retrieves history from a separate memory bank and still denoises future latents with a separate world model shi2026memoryvlapp . OmniDreams, the causal backbone we build on, reports preliminary results for a policy that runs it once per decision nvidia2026omnidreams , but that policy reads the backbone through a single token and is not described as reusing computation across decisions. Motivated by these gaps, AR-WAM pairs a cache of observed history with the rollout-free pass above, so that neither history encoding nor future denoising is repeated at a decision. title: DailyBrick: Language-Guided Synthesis of Brick Assembly Instructions
summary: Generating a LEGO model from a user request is more than a plausible 3D shape generation. LEGO models require physical support per brick, and each brick should be placed unblocked. Current methods address this issue by training an expert large language model. We reduce the problem of generating extremely long context on all brick connections to that of writing a program that builds LEGO models like a human, considering each intermediate step could be executed. We introduce DailyBrick , a multi-stage agentic system that produces a LEGO model together with a brick-by-brick assembly instruction for human building and robot assembly. We design a multi-stage harness with roles to help LLMs generate more effectively. A versioned construction SDK compiles multi-level decisions, from semantic subparts to individual bricks, into canonical operations. An external Meta-Reviewer agent replays and inspects the generated package, verifies the model and its construction process, identifies failures, traces them to the responsible stage, and routes them to bounded repairs or to editable candidates for later skill or tool updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DailyBrick generates LEGO models based on simple user requests better than recent agentic systems, and show its utility in downstream applications such as robot manipulations on model assembly from instructions and brick sets (https://SpatialAgent.github.io/DailyBrick/).

Introduction Recent advances in 3D generation have made it possible to create diverse object models from text or images. For objects built from multiple parts, however, generating the final geometry does not by itself specify how those parts should be assembled. Assembly connects a desired object to a sequence of actions and intermediate steps, making it a useful setting for studying long-horizon planning, robot manipulation, and error recovery in embodied systems~ sener2022assembly101,heo2023furniturebench . Generating an object together with its assembly instructions could therefore provide both manuals for a human builder and downstream tasks for robot manipulation. Extending this goal to arbitrary real-world objects is challenging because their parts vary in geometry, connection mechanisms, and physical requirements. LEGO offers a controlled yet expressive setting for studying this problem. Its standardized catalogue defines atomic bricks with fixed geometries and specified connections, while their combinations support diverse objects and structural layouts~ pun2025brickgpt,kulits2026bricknet . This setting allows us to study the generation of both a model and the brick-by-brick sequence that constructs it. Even with standardized bricks, a plausible LEGO model does not guarantee an executable assembly instruction. Each step must be compatible with the current partial assembly, making construction depend on both the spatial arrangement of bricks and their placement order. Existing approaches address different aspects of this problem. Image2Lego~ lennon2021image2lego directly fills a final voxel volume with bricks, while ASAP~ tian2024asap plans assembly sequences for known parts and target poses through disassembly search. BrickGPT~ pun2025brickgpt integrates validity checks and physics-aware rollback into autoregressive brick generation. LegoACE~ xu2025legoace encodes each brick as tokens, yet its authors report that some outputs remain disconnected. BrickNet~ kulits2026bricknet further represents typed connections and checks construction prefixes for connectivity and collision. These methods advance assembly planning and model generation, but identifying an invalid step does not by itself determine which construction decision should be revised. A failed step may stem from a brick's pose, an incompatible design, or an earlier structural plan. Linking the failure to the decisions that produced it is therefore important for targeted refinement. Recent agentic workflows offer a way by decomposing long-context generation into structured stages with intermediate outputs and feedback, enabling iterative refinement of generation programs~ yao2022react,hong2023metagpt,wang2024codeact . General-purpose coding agents such as Claude Code~ claude , Codex~ codex , and DeepSeek Harness~ deepseekharness can plan, write, and iteratively refine software with limited human supervision. ReAct~ yao2022react and CodeAct~ wang2024codeact connect language-model reasoning to tool use and executable actions, while MetaGPT~ hong2023metagpt coordinates specialized agent roles. In 3D generation, SceneSmith~ pfaff2026scenesmith organizes scene construction into hierarchical stages, and Articraft~ zhou2026articraft uses executable programs and feedback to refine generated designs. Applying these ideas to brick assembly requires connecting high-level structural decisions to individual placements, so that a failed construction step can be traced back to the decisions that produced it. Motivated by these observations, we introduce , an agentic pipeline that turns user requests into LEGO models and their step-by-step assembly instructions , reviewing each step and locating errors back to target stages or programs that need refinements. organizes the pipeline as a sequence of bounded stages, from overall layouts and semantic subpart designs to individual brick placement. A Planner-Designer-Critic workflow with separate contexts at each stage, passing only committed stage outputs to the next. Moreover, a Self Meta-Reviewer uses replay and provenance evidence to route detected defects to the implicated stage and stage output. It decides whether the current package(models and instructions) can be accepted or should trigger an update. Additionally, to bridge agents' semantic planning and executable brick operations on LEGO models, we propose a versioned Software Development Kit (SDK). It supports both individual steps (colours, directions, brick ID) with partial assembly skills, allowing agents to express object-level plans as traceable step-by-step assembly instructions. Moreover, Self Meta-Reviewer replays the instructions to verify the result and locates errors in incomplete replay to update related stage, skills, or tools for refinement. We develop a brick-construction SDK with reusable partial assembly skills and traceable brick operations. Combined with verify replay, these operations provide evidence for the Self Meta-Reviewer to locate errors and guide targeted updates. Extensive experiments across multiple base models demonstrate that could improve LEGO model generation in visual quality and assembly-sequence validity, while simulation examples illustrate downstream assembly and interaction. title: When the World Is the Test Suite: Agentic Intelligence for the Physical World
summary: Coding agents built to repair software now write, test, and repair programs for robots, laboratories, and industrial controllers. Unlike in software engineering, no test suite comes with the code. Whether a program works must be established by running it on a robot, in a physics simulator, or through the policies it helps to train, and such evidence is costly to obtain and can itself be wrong. As these agents take on more physical tasks, how their programs are judged matters as much as how they are written. This paper examines this emerging area, agentic intelligence for the physical world, by treating the world as the program's test suite. We organize the discussion around three questions: how agents write programs for the physical world, how these programs are tested, and how agents learn from the results. We first trace how language models for robots and software engineering agents came together, ask which software testing practices carry over to physical tests, and describe each program by where it sits relative to the actuator and by what judges it. For writing, we cover programs that act as robot policies and programs that support policy learning by producing rewards, tasks, and training worlds. For testing, we examine what physical trials cost, what traces, learned judges, simulators, and formal checks can establish in their place, and what safety requires beyond task success. For learning, we discuss how tested programs are retained as experience, in skill libraries and in model weights. Finally, we turn to benchmarks and evaluation practice and outline open challenges. Writing programs is becoming cheap, while trustworthy evidence about what they do remains costly. Progress will therefore depend on a physical counterpart of continuous integration: verification cheap enough to run often, reliable enough to trust under search, and maintained alongside the experience it validates.

Introduction sec:introduction A coding agent is trying to put a moka pot on a stove. It is looking at four images taken just before and just after a simulated gripper attempted to grasp the pot's handle. The fingers have closed on empty air beside it. The agent rereads the grasp routine it wrote an hour earlier and sees that it aimed at the center of the pot's segmentation mask. It changes the target to the handle and runs the program again from fifty initial states. The pot is lifted in most of them. The agent writes a short note describing the failure and its fix and adds it to a library that agents working on other tasks will read. This is a composite scene with illustrative details, but systems such as ASPIRE already carry out this sequence of inspection, repair, validation, and reuse arxiv260700272 . draws the scene as a loop. The debugging loop is familiar from software engineering: run the program, inspect the failure, revise it, rerun it, and keep what works arxiv240515793,arxiv240716741,arxiv231006770 . Recent robotics systems reuse general-purpose coding agents for this work, giving them access to robot interfaces and execution environments. On manipulation benchmarks with task perturbations, these systems report success rates well above those published for end-to-end policies trained on demonstrations arxiv260700272,arxiv260616458,arxiv261002459 . Validated programs can also generate successful trajectories for training those policies arxiv260929166,arxiv260927308 . In the opening scene, lifting the pot still leaves the task unfinished. Has the pot reached the burner, and is it upright and stable? The claim that it was lifted also depends on what the agent can observe and on what counts as a successful lift. In many software tasks, an existing test suite gives the agent a cheap, repeatable check on a proposed repair. For a physical task, the check may require observations, simulator state, or another trial, and its cost and reliability depend on how it is made. The literature shows both the value of execution feedback and the expense of obtaining it. In ASPIRE's ablation on LIBERO-PRO, an execution engine and a skill library together raise macro-average success from 14 to 62 . The engine records perception and control calls, exposes images before and after them, and re-runs candidate repairs. Evolutionary search then adds another 10 percentage points arxiv260700272 . For programs that generate training environments, useful feedback can require training a policy on the environments they produce. A full Eurekaverse run incurs about 15 US dollars in language-model API costs and takes about 24 hours on eight A6000 GPUs arxiv241101775 . Beyond its cost, the judgment itself can be wrong zhao-etal-2025-codejudge,zeng-etal-2025-mm,lin-etal-2025-fact,kong-etal-2025-sharp,arxiv261029677 . On FailBench, the best of thirteen detectors based on vision-language models (VLMs) reaches a macro-averaged balanced accuracy of only 0.77 when judging manipulation outcomes arxiv260903611 . In OpenRUA's analysis of failed episodes, about a quarter involve a success condition absent from the instruction or a predicate that contradicts it arxiv261002459 . These results motivate our central claim: for agents that write programs for the physical world, obtaining trustworthy evidence about program behavior is increasingly a limiting factor. We examine how this problem arises, what the available evidence supports, and how it shapes the design of agents, their memory, and their evaluation. compares this article with existing reviews on five points: coverage of the physical world, programs as the object of study, analysis of judges, coverage of laboratory and industrial code, and transfer from software practice. Reviews of foundation models in robotics and of vision-language-action models organize the field by capability or by the form of the action, with code as one action representation or a planning tool arxiv231107226,arxiv231208782,arxiv231207843,arxiv231210807,arxiv240205741,arxiv240514093,arxiv250701925 . Reviews of code generation and of software-engineering agents cover execution feedback and testing in depth but leave the physical world out arxiv240600515,arxiv240902977 . Three recent reviews come closest. Weights or Skills? contrasts policies stored in weights with agents that write their own code skills, orders code-as-policy systems by their degree of self-improvement, and proposes metrics for cumulative improvement arxiv260801851 . No Free Checker reviews about 150 verifiers of robot policies and identifies a trade-off between the availability and credibility of their judgments arxiv260909250 . Code as Agent Harness treats code as the executable substrate of agents in general, names embodied agents and self-driving laboratories among its applications, and observes that ``execution is only as reliable as the oracle attached to it'' arxiv260518747 . This article takes as its object of comparison the program in the physical world, together with the evidence that judges it. The Weights or Skills? review follows how much a code-writing agent improves, and we ask what certified each improvement. No Free Checker grades verifiers of policies, whereas our concern is the judges of programs, artifacts that can be read, traced, and repaired. From the software machinery that Code as Agent Harness catalogs, we pick out the parts that survive contact with robots, laboratories, and industrial controllers. A framework and survey from October 2026, Who Improves the Robot?, also comes close. It argues that no robot work it surveys yet demonstrates independently verified recursive self-improvement arxiv261018842 . That survey assesses claims of self-improvement as a whole, whereas we compare the evidence behind individual programs. Concretely, this article makes four contributions: [leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt] We describe each program by where it sits relative to the actuator and by what judges it, and use these two properties to compare representative systems from action code to generated training worlds. We compare programs with end-to-end policies across the reported studies, which favor programs when the structure of a task changes and in several long-horizon and constrained settings. We also set out what traces, judges, simulators, and formal checks can each establish about a program, and collect the documented failure modes of every kind of judge. We examine how accepted programs become retained experience, in skill libraries and in model weights, and identify five quantities that are needed to distinguish progress from regression and that current reports rarely state: cost, variance, judge visibility, judge error, and the link between simulation and reality. We ask which software testing practices carry over to physical tests and which break, and set out open problems, each paired with a first experiment. The Physical World as a Test Suite sec:lens sec:foundations We call the subject agentic intelligence for the physical world: work in which a model writes or edits a program whose effects are evaluated through physical execution on a robot, in a physics simulator, or through a policy trained with the program's output. Where physical trial is not permitted, a model of the equipment the program controls can take the place of execution. shows the loop that these systems share. A model writes a program, the program runs in physical dynamics, a judge decides from what happened whether the program succeeded, and that result either guides a repair or adds the program to a skill library that later programs reuse. Each step of this loop has a counterpart in software engineering, where an agent edits a patch, executes it, checks the result against a test oracle, and merges a change that later work builds on. There, a test suite ties running, judging, and keeping together: it usually comes with the repository, and the agent can run it after every edit. Treating the physical world as the test suite means asking, at every step of the loop, what the world supplies in place of a test: which observations count as evidence, what an evaluation costs, how often a judgment is wrong, and what an accepted change commits later work to. To compare programs across this loop, we describe each one by two coordinates, defined in : where the program sits relative to the robot's actuators, and what judges it. Three research questions follow from the loop: : What do programs buy an agent that acts in the physical world, and what do they cost? Where in the stack should the program sit, when does it outperform an end-to-end policy, and how should the two be combined? : When the world is the test suite, how do agents learn that a program is wrong, and how far can that signal be trusted? What do traces, judges, simulators, and formal checks contribute, and what replaces physical trial when trial is not allowed? : How does validated experience accumulate, and what shows that progress is real? When do skill libraries help or hurt, how far does their content transfer, and what must be reported for a result to be interpretable? maps the article onto the loop, with representative work for each part. Before comparing methods, we define the scope with a running example, trace how coding agents entered this work, examine what carries over from software testing ( ), and set out the program roles and evaluation sources used for comparison. title: Beyond Episodic Recall: Experience-to-Knowledge Evolution for Lifelong Embodied Navigation
summary: Lifelong embodied navigation requires agents to accumulate experience through continuous interaction and reuse it for subsequent goal searches. Existing memory-enhanced methods typically retain historical observations or construct structured scene representations. However, storing observations or high-dimensional semantic embeddings incurs growing storage costs. Meanwhile, structured representations support retrieval and semantic reasoning but do not explicitly evolve accumulated experience into environment-specific knowledge. To address these limitations, we propose Experience-Evolving Memory (EvoNav), a novel two-timescale memory framework. It organizes semantic observations, spatial relations, and task-feedback cues into sparse experience atoms. During online operation, experience atoms continually consolidate repeated observations and form dynamic links based on transitions. At the slower timescale, EvoNav distills accumulated category co-occurrences and feedback signals into environment-specific structural knowledge without relying on predefined object--room relations. For each new goal, EvoNav combines direct goal evidence from experience atoms with learned structural knowledge to guide goal-directed search on the current traversability map. Experiments on single-goal, sequential multi-floor, and multimodal navigation demonstrate effective experience reuse and improved path efficiency with compact persistent memory, together with successful transfer to a real robot.

Introduction sec:evonav_intro Zero-shot ObjectNav systems combine semantic mapping with goal-directed exploration to search unfamiliar scenes~ zhou2023esc,yu2023l3mvn,yokoyama2024vlfm . Practical agents, however, often execute successive goals in the same multi-floor environment, where past observations and traversal can inform later search. This calls for accumulating reusable knowledge across tasks~ wani2020multion,chang2024goat . Existing memory-enhanced navigation methods represent past experience in several forms. Image-based methods directly retain visual snapshots or multi-view observations for later retrieval~ yang2025threedmem,wang2026lmee . Feature-based methods project language-aligned semantic embeddings into 3D space, producing spatial feature maps that support open-vocabulary queries~ huang2023vlmaps,peng2023openscene,jatavallabhula2023conceptfusion . Other methods adopt structured representations, organizing perceived entities, spatial topology, and interaction history into object-relation, hierarchical, or persistent memory graphs for semantic reasoning and decision-making~ gu2024conceptgraphs,rana2023sayplan,werby2024hovsg,niu2026ssmgnav,chen2026stegnav . In multi-floor environments, 3D traversability modeling and floor connectivity further make cross-floor navigation decisions executable~ zheng2026travexplorer,li2026lifelongcrossnav . Together, these directions establish important foundations for experience reuse, structured reasoning, and cross-floor sequential navigation. Despite this progress, a gap remains, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:evonav_motivation , between lightweight experience accumulation and learning environment-specific structural knowledge. Accumulating visual observations and high-dimensional spatial features increases storage and maintenance costs as interaction grows~ yang2025threedmem , but their immediate value is often limited to relocating a previously observed target. Scene graphs are commonly designed to organize perceptual entities or provide task-time relational context, focusing on semantic reasoning and decision-making rather than distilling repeated traversal and task outcomes into compact, feedback-calibrated memory~ gu2024conceptgraphs,yin2024sgnav,yin2025unigoal,huang2026msgnav . Likewise, external commonsense priors can guide exploration~ zhou2023esc,yu2023l3mvn , but may not reflect the structure of the current environment~ zhang2023layout . In contrast, repeated object co-occurrences, behavior-supported transitions, and task feedback provide direct signals for learning how a particular environment is organized. We therefore ask: how can an agent retain reusable navigation experience compactly, and evolve it into environment-specific knowledge that guides subsequent searches? Inspired by two-timescale learning~ mahadevan2026convergence , we formulate a memory-learning paradigm coupling fast online consolidation with slow environment-specific knowledge evolution. Accordingly, we propose EvoNav, a two-timescale experience-to-knowledge framework for lifelong embodied navigation. Drawing on the atomic notes and dynamic links of Zettelkasten~ kadavy2021digitalzettelkasten,xu2025amem , EvoNav represents local interactions as sparse experience atoms containing semantic, spatial, relational, and feedback cues without imposing a fixed object=room hierarchy. At the fast timescale, online experience consolidation merges repeated observations into existing atoms and maintains perceptual and behavior-supported transition links. At the slow timescale, experience-to-knowledge evolution transforms these atom-level relations into environment-specific category-level co-occurrence and transition patterns, while task outcomes calibrate the goal-conditioned reliability of each atom. For each new goal, Atom=Graph Evidence Propagation (AGEP) combines direct atom evidence with learned structural support. The fused evidence is then propagated over perceptual and transition links to rank relevant atoms. Atom=object binding and traversability checks then ground the selected atoms into executable navigation targets. Our main contributions are as follows: Sparse experience atom memory. We introduce sparse experience atoms that compactly encode navigation-relevant semantic, spatial, and feedback cues, without relying on a fixed object-room hierarchy or persistently storing visual snapshots and per-voxel high-dimensional semantic features. Memory evolution across timescales. We coordinate online experience consolidation with slower experience-to-knowledge evolution, integrating repeated observations into experience and learning environment-specific structural knowledge from co-occurrences, behavioral transitions, and task feedback for subsequent searches. Experience-graph reasoning and grounded navigation. We combine direct evidence with learned structural support, using atom-ObjectMap binding and feasibility checks on the current traversability map to turn historical experience into actionable navigation candidates across tasks and floors. Comprehensive evaluation and real-world deployment. Experiments on single-goal, sequential multi-floor, and multimodal navigation demonstrate strong path efficiency with a compact persistent-memory footprint. Deployment on a real mobile robot further validates the feasibility of the system. title: SR-VLA: Stall-Reduced VLA Execution via Predicted-Input Lookahead and Selective KV Cache Repair
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur control stalls when inference blocks the next action chunk. Asynchronous early inference can hide latency, but its results may be inconsistent with the arriving actual inputs. Unconditional reuse risks acting on mismatched inputs, whereas full recomputation discards useful precomputation. We propose SR-VLA, combining predicted-input lookahead with selective KV cache repair. During current chunk execution, a lightweight action-conditioned predictor generates next-boundary visual observations and proprioceptive state. These predictions, together with the task instruction, drive the frozen VLA to precompute a speculative KV cache and action chunk. After real inputs are available to VLA, predicted--real differences and task conditions determine whether to accept the action chunk or trigger selective KV repair. On LIBERO, SR-VLA achieves $2.67\times$ and $1.27\times$ query speedups over the respective synchronous $π_{0.5}$ and OpenVLA-OFT baselines, while maintaining competitive average task success rates. Under target-motion perturbation, success remains baseline-comparable, with $1.52\times$--$1.93\times$ query speedup.

However, each decision requires a complete inference over the latest inputs, resulting in substantial inference latency that limits the real-time responsiveness of robotic systems. Existing studies have explored multiple directions to alleviate this latency. One line of work lowers the cost of an individual VLA forward pass through compact model design or quantization tinyvla,qail , as well as pruning or adaptive computation spvla,dyslvla,efficientvla,flashvla . Another line reduces VLA invocation frequency through action chunking act,openvlaoft , or accelerates action generation through parallel or speculative decoding parallelvla,specvla,kerv . title: VoxelSBFL: Voxel-Level Spectrum-Based Failure Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation to control robots. Testing these systems produces trajectories and task outcomes, but existing approaches provide limited guidance on using these recorded trajectories to assess subsequent executions or inform policy repair. We conjecture that, for a given policy and task, traversing certain workspace regions is associated with a higher likelihood of failure. To investigate this conjecture, we propose VoxelSBFL, a black-box adaptation of Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) in which workspace voxels replace program elements as units of analysis. Recorded tool-center-point (TCP) trajectories provide binary voxel coverage, which is combined with execution outcomes to construct suspiciousness maps using established SBFL formulas. These maps identify failure-associated regions and score unseen trajectories without requiring internal model access. We evaluate 34 spectrum-based techniques across four VLA models using 96,000 Pick-Up trajectories in simulation and compare the leading techniques against eight action- and trajectory-based metrics. VoxelSBFL obtains an overall macro ROC-AUC of 0.704, significantly outperforming state-of-the art baselines. Sensitivity analyses show that performance varies with spatial granularity and training-set size. These findings support spatial spectra for VLA execution assessment and motivate future research on runtime monitoring, self-healing and targeted policy improvement.

Models such as the GR00T-N1 VLA family~ nvidia2025gr00tn1openfoundation and ~ black2024pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel translate visual observations and natural-language instructions into robotic actions. Within the complete robotic stack, these actions are executed by low-level controllers, producing trajectories through the physical workspace. Therefore, assessing the reliability of VLA-enabled robots requires understanding when and under which conditions their executions fail. To support this assessment, recent approaches have proposed different testing methods, including test generation approaches~ wang2025vlatest,kanwal2026fatevla or methods that aim to deal with the test oracle problem~ valle2026metamorphic,valle2026mango . However, once these tests have been executed and their outcomes determined, existing testing approaches offer limited guidance on how to use the recorded trajectories to predict failures in subsequent executions or inform policy repair. Certain approaches aim at predicting failures during VLA executions. For instance, Valle et al.~ valle2025evaluating propose both white-box and black-box approaches to distinguish successful and failed executions or high, medium or low quality task executions. SAFE~ gu2026safe and VLA-Tug~ podolinsky2026failure rely on internal VLA representations, restricting their use to policies that expose those representations. VLA-Tug also uses annotated failure onsets during training. Nevertheless, these approaches have certain limitations. From the debugging perspective, the scores and alerts produced by these methods give developers limited guidance and explainability of under what circumstances the VLA fails. From the practical perspectives, some of such approaches require internal access to the VLA policy (e.g., white-box uncertainty metrics from~ valle2025evaluating , internal VLA activations at each policy step for obtaining training data~ podolinsky2026failure ), which is not always easy to obtain. r 0.65 Spatial Distribution of Successful and Failed Robot Trajectories fig:failuredistr Figure fig:failuredistr shows the robot’s end-effector trajectories in three dimensions (left) and projected onto the 2D X-Y plane (right), with failed executions shown in red and successful ones in green for the model. The 2D projection makes the spatial pattern particularly clear. Failed trajectories predominate in the upper region outlined in red, while successful trajectories predominate in the right-hand region outlined in green. We therefore conjecture that, in VLA-enabled robots, traversing certain regions of the workspace is associated with a higher likelihood of task failure. This conjecture draws on an analogy with conventional software. A test that executes a faulty statement may be more likely to fail because certain inputs or program states can trigger the fault. Similarly, a robot execution may be more likely to fail when the end effector passes through a problematic region of the workspace. This analogy motivates treating the regions visited by a robot as a form of coverage, much like the statements executed by a software test. Building on this intuition, we propose VoxelSBFL, which recasts failure prediction for VLA-enabled robots as a spatial adaptation of spectrum-based fault localization (SBFL)~ jones2002visualization . We partition the robot’s three-dimensional workspace into voxels and use these voxels in place of program elements. Just as a software test covers a statement by executing it, a robot trajectory covers a voxel if at least one recorded position of the end effector’s tool center point falls within it. We combine this voxel coverage information with the success or failure outcome of each execution and apply standard SBFL formulas to quantify how strongly coverage of each voxel is associated with failure. The resulting suspiciousness map highlights workspace regions that warrant closer inspection. Developers can use it to identify segments of failed trajectories to examine, including the actions and observations that preceded entry into a highly suspicious voxel. The same map could guide the generation of new trajectories that exercise these regions and the collection of successful demonstrations for targeted repair (e.g., through policy fine-tuning). In this study, we evaluate how well the map distinguishes successful from failed executions, as a proof to determine whether spectrum-based techniques can be employed in this context. We evaluate how well VoxelSBFL distinguishes successful from failed executions using complete, held-out trajectories. We compare 34 SBFL formulas on 96,000 simulated executions across four state-of-the-art VLA models and benchmark the leading formulas against eight other black-box metrics proposed by Valle et al. valle2025evaluating , including action- and trajectory-based metrics. Harmonic Mean and Rogot2 achieve the highest macro-averaged ROC-AUC among the SBFL formulas (0.704), outperforming the strongest motion-instability baseline (0.655). We also find that voxel size affects the relative ranking of the formulas and that Harmonic Mean improves as more labeled trajectories are used to construct the map. title: CueSplat: Learning to Schedule Sparse Deformation for Dynamic Gaussian Splatting on Edge Devices
summary: Deformation-based 4D Gaussian splatting (4DGS) enables dynamic scene rendering. However, evaluating deformation networks for all Gaussians at every frame is compute-intensive on edge devices. We find that Gaussian trajectories are often locally predictable, yet prediction reliability varies across Gaussians and time. Thus, we propose CueSplat, a post-training framework that exploits local temporal regularity while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen and retaining its Gaussian set. Specifically, CueSplat predicts Gaussian attributes from recent history and uses a lightweight learned router to select exact deformation updates within a scene-specific budget calibrated offline. Selection accounts for prediction reliability and rendering contribution. Selected indices are reused across nearby frames to reduce routing overhead, while selected Gaussians still receive exact updates each frame. To control accumulated prediction error, we use drift signals to schedule three consecutive full-deformation frames that rebuild the prediction history. Evaluated across four mainstream 4DGS algorithms, CueSplat achieves up to $6.74\times$ and $8.15\times$ speedups on Jetson AGX Orin and Orin NX, respectively, with a negligible quality drop (at most $0.16$ dB in dataset-average PSNR).

In mainstream 4DGS, a deformation network transforms Gaussians into their states at a given timestamp. Then, the resulting Gaussians are projected and rendered to a targeted viewpoint. Bottleneck. However, evaluating the deformation network for all Gaussians at every frame is costly on edge devices. For E-D3DGS~ bae2024ed3dgs on Jetson AGX Orin, deformation accounts for about 85 of GPU pipeline time on N3DV~ li2022neuralvideo . Existing methods reduce computation through Gaussian pruning~ tu2026speede , static--dynamic decomposition~ chen2025dash,lee2024explicit , or shared motion representations~ huang2024scgs,kratimenos2024dynmf,kwak2025modec . Nevertheless, reducing the Gaussian set or restricting motion expressiveness can compromise reconstruction quality. Static–dynamic partitions also remain fixed during rendering, and misclassifying dynamic Gaussians as static can degrade motion reconstruction. Our approach retains the pretrained Gaussian set and deformation model, combining temporal prediction with adaptive selection of deformation updates. Insight. There is a long history of leveraging short-term temporal regularity in various video-based applications~ bewley2016sort,liu2017voxelflow . All these approaches use recent history states to predict future states. Our key insight here is that many Gaussian trajectories exhibit local temporal regularity ( ). This motivates us to leverage temporal extrapolation from recent history. However, prediction reliability varies across Gaussians and over time, and the impact of a state error on the rendered image depends on visibility and rendering contribution. These observations motivate selecting Gaussians for exact updates based on prediction reliability and rendering contribution. Method. Based on our insight, we propose , a post-training acceleration framework ( ) that enables sparse Gaussian deformation while keeping the pretrained 4DGS model intact without pruning. During inference, a lightweight router periodically selects a subset of Gaussians for exact deformation updates. For the remaining Gaussians, we predict their states from the three most recent accepted states. We merge the exact deformation outputs for the selected Gaussians with the predicted states of the remaining Gaussians for rendering. In addition, to improve the rendering efficiency, we further reuse the indices of the Gaussian subset across nearby frames to reduce routing overhead, while deformation is recomputed for the selected Gaussians at each frame. title: Progress Predicts Policy
summary: A task specifies how the world should change, while a policy specifies what the robot should do. We introduce Progress Predicts Policy (PPP), which learns a language-conditioned scalar field through the commands induced by its differential. We obtain action conditioning by composing a latent progress field with a shared world model and read its action gradient at a fixed reference command. Continuous commands scale this gradient by a learned positive gain, while discrete commands use finite differences of the same scalar. This yields a hybrid policy without a separate action head or iterative search. Fitting demonstration progress values alone does not ensure that action gradients align with expert commands. PPP trains the induced commands by imitation and uses double backpropagation for the continuous gradient readout to shape the field's local control geometry. Demonstration timing calibrates field values on observed states without additional annotation. The continuous readout remains learnable without progress labels but these timing-derived targets support progress monitoring during execution. Experiments in simulated and real robot manipulation show that PPP outperforms behavioral cloning under a shared architecture.

title: InteractVLA: Turning VLAs into Interactive Tools for Agentic Robotic Manipulation
summary: Existing agentic manipulation systems treat pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies as opaque, language-only primitives: when a policy call fails under unfamiliar instructions or scene perturbations, the agent cannot steer its behavior and is forced into futile retries or costly manual takeover. We present InteractVLA, a framework that turns pretrained flow-based VLAs into geometrically steerable and inspectable tools through a bidirectional geometric interface with vision-language agents. In the forward direction, test-time geometric guidance translates an agent-specified end-effector target into input gradients through the action expert via a differentiable command-to-pose mapping, while soft-time target alignment treats arrival time as a latent execution index to match the target pose without distorting the policy's approach motion. In the reverse direction, action-informed agentic refinement exposes generated action chunks and calibrated camera reprojections back to the agent, allowing it to diagnose spatial discrepancies, revise targets for subsequent VLA calls, or locally adjust motion segments on top of the guided trajectory. Making the VLA controllable not only boosts online agentic tool use, but also unlocks effective recursive self-improvement (RSI), achieving state-of-the-art performance of 99.4\% on LIBERO-Plus, 48.62\% on RoboDojo, and 89.4\% on RoboCasa365.
