Introduction Combining vision-language agents with pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies promises an appealing division of labor for robotic manipulation: the agent handles long-horizon reasoning and task decomposition, while the VLA provides temporally coherent motor execution~ harness,rvicl . Yet in practice, existing VLAs hardly function as true interactive tools. Because standard VLAs only accept high-level language instructions and operate as opaque black boxes, the agent cannot steer how the policy executes a skill~ zhou2025libero,li2026roborecover . When a VLA call fails, simply commanding a retry is largely futile because it produces nearly identical motions under similar observations, whereas rephrasing the language instruction often pushes the VLA out of distribution and sharply degrades success (Figure~ fig:img1 , middle). Across scenarios requiring generalization, the agent cannot rely on the VLA and must take over low-level control entirely, acting as a fallback supervisor that cleans up after an uncontrollable policy rather than a planner wielding a reliable tool~ zhou2026improves,qu2026roboharness, choi2026vla,xu2026vla . This limitation stems from an inadequate interface between high-level reasoning and low-level control. Even when unfamiliar instructions or scene layouts prevent a VLA from grounding the right target, its pretrained spatial perception and motor priors, such as smooth approach trajectories, coordinated rotations, and grasp timing, remain highly capable~ bai2025evolve,li2026simplevla . As shown in Figure~ fig:img1 (right), explicitly steering the end effector toward the intended interaction target allows the exact same policy to redirect its manipulation behavior and complete the task while preserving execution precision. Turning a VLA into a genuinely usable tool therefore requires moving beyond language-only invocation to a bidirectional geometric interface: the agent must be able to specify explicit spatial targets to guide the VLA's action generation, and conversely inspect the resulting motion proposals to refine subsequent execution~ pu2026tgm,chancan20253d,weng2026interaction . Building such a bidirectional interface at test time poses two coupled challenges. In the forward direction (Agent VLA), the agent supplies a sparse target configuration to approach rather than a dense trajectory or exact arrival time. While the VLA should synthesize the intervening motion, naively applying a fixed-time penalty pulls the wrong execution step toward the target, whereas penalizing every step uniformly collapses the approach trajectory altogether. In the reverse direction (VLA Agent), a binary success or failure signal is insufficient for recovery. Once guided by an agent-specified target, the VLA's generated action chunk already reflects the agent's spatial intent. By comparing the executed prefix and unexecuted continuation against visual observations, the agent can determine whether a failure requires calling the VLA again with a revised target or merely applying a lightweight local adjustment to the policy's well-structured trajectory, making recovery far more tractable than full manual takeover. To address these challenges, we introduce InteractVLA, a framework that turns pretrained flow-based VLAs into geometrically steerable and inspectable tools for agentic manipulation (Figure~ fig:teaser ). Drawing on VLM-based policy steering~ vls and visual geometric constraints~ voxposer,rekep , InteractVLA bridges agent reasoning and action generation through three components. First, test-time geometric guidance uses a differentiable command-to-pose mapping to translate an agent-specified end-effector target (position, orientation, and gripper state) into input gradients through the action expert within a single denoising trajectory, reshaping motion toward the agent's intent while returning control early if low confidence indicates an incompatible target. Second, soft-time target alignment formulates arrival time as a latent execution index, jointly matching complete target poses at a shared arrival step that emerges naturally as the trajectory takes shape. Third, action-informed agentic refinement exposes generated action chunks alongside calibrated camera reprojections and execution history to the agent, enabling it to diagnose spatial discrepancies, revise subsequent targets, or locally edit motion segments. Because InteractVLA makes the VLA steerable rather than rigidly repeating a single action mode, it also provides a strong foundation for recursive self-improvement (RSI): across attempts, the agent iteratively sharpens how it specifies geometric targets and refines policy-generated motions. Across LIBERO-Plus~ liberoplus , RoboDojo~ robodojo , RoboCasa365~ robocasa365 , and real-world manipulation, InteractVLA substantially outperforms standalone VLAs, language-only agent-VLA baselines, while reducing token consumption by over an order of magnitude compared with step-by-step agent-only control. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce InteractVLA, a framework that turns pretrained VLAs into interactive, controllable tools for agents via test-time geometric guidance, soft-time target alignment, and action-informed agentic refinement. We show that making VLAs geometrically steerable and inspectable unlocks effective recursive self-improvement (RSI), allowing agents to progressively refine target specification and motion correction. We achieve state-of-the-art performance across LIBERO-Plus (99.4 ), RoboDojo (48.62 ), and RoboCasa365 (89.4 ), with real-world evaluations confirming consistent gains in manipulation success and efficiency. title: EgoHandWAM: Probing the Role of Hand Motion in Egocentric World Action Modeling
summary: How much does hand motion tell us about what a first-person camera will see next? EgoHandWAM forecasts three-dimensional wrist and fingertip trajectories and a future visual feature from the current image and recent hand states. We train on 751,065 EgoDex windows using a frozen DINOv2 encoder. On held-out development sessions, the action-only model reduces two-second wrist endpoint error from 60.26 to 56.48~mm relative to a stationary forecast. It still underestimates long reaches. Adding future-feature supervision gives nearly identical trajectory accuracy. With the recorded hand history, the visual head reduces smooth L1 error by 1.32\% relative to copying the current feature. Shuffling histories across sessions erases this gain. In a separate four-task probe, adding recorded future displacements to observed context and future tracking-validity masks reduces visual-feature error by 3.93\%. Masks alone give little improvement. A trajectory predicted from the same observations adds little. On two simulated RoboTwin tasks, substituting aligned human examples for an auxiliary batch of robot examples gives no consistent increase in task success across three training seeds.

Introduction introduction When someone reaches for a lid, a first-person camera records the hand, the object and the motion of the camera itself. A wrist trajectory captures part of this interaction. How much can a model anticipate before the hand moves, and how useful is that information for predicting what comes into view? Ego4D and EgoDex make it possible to study these questions in recorded human activity ref-ego4d,ref-egodex . We examine hand motion in three roles. First, motion is a prediction target. Given the current image and eight observed hand states, EgoHandWAM predicts the next two seconds of wrist and fingertip positions. A second head predicts the visual feature at the last time step. We vary the weight of the visual loss while holding the trajectories, inputs and training budget fixed. Second, motion is an input to a visual forecast. A separate regression model receives either a recorded future trajectory with its tracking mask or a trajectory predicted from the observed context. Comparing these inputs distinguishes information available after the movement from information a model can supply at prediction time. Third, human recordings provide auxiliary training data for a robot policy. A shared Transformer learns from human and robot observations, while simulated demonstrations supervise the robot commands. We measure task completion in simulated bottle grasping and bimanual block handover, and test whether the correspondence between a human hand history and its video matters. Only robot demonstrations supply executable action labels. summary: Robot demonstrations are collected on different embodiments, leaving many robot-skill combinations unobserved. Pooling these data shares visual knowledge, while joint labels remain tied to the demonstrating kinematic chain. We propose a geometry-supervised training framework for zero-shot composition of familiar robots and skills. The central insight is that a demonstrated command provides a tool-space target for every robot that can realize it. Calibrated forward kinematics supplies this supervision to foreign native action interfaces without their joint labels for that skill. Native reconstruction retains demonstrated configurations, and positive reachability checks select targets for cross-robot supervision. A visual policy learns to predict shared actions and executes through the target robot's native decoder. Introduction Suppose one robot learns to place a cup on a shelf and another learns to place containers in a drawer. Each has practiced grasping, transporting and releasing objects. A shared policy has also seen both tasks. Yet asking the second robot to place the cup introduces a missing combination of a familiar robot and a familiar skill. This gap is common when robot datasets are assembled from separate platforms, environments and collection efforts. Collecting every task on every robot scales with the product of the two sets. Reusing demonstrations requires a way for supervision from an observed combination to inform a missing one. The action labels make this difficult. A joint vector describes how the demonstrating robot moves. Its entries depend on joint count, link geometry, joint conventions and installation. Even when two arms have the same number of joints, equal numerical commands can move their tools differently. A shared model can learn useful transfer from images, language and repeated task structure, but native labels provide no explicit correspondence between these different motions. Padding labels to a common width makes them compatible with a network input or output. The remaining learning problem is to connect their physical meanings. Known robot geometry supplies a physical correspondence. A demonstrated joint command determines the calibrated tool's position, orientation and opening in a shared task frame. For another robot, this target constrains the effect of its action while leaving its joint solution to its own kinematic chain. One source demonstration can therefore supervise several native action interfaces, including those without demonstrations of the source task. The required information is the robots' geometry and calibration, together with evidence that a foreign chain can reach the target. Figure~ fig:teaser illustrates how this supervision can connect familiar robots and skills across missing combinations. Our approach learns native action interfaces around this supervision path. A source action is encoded into shared coordinates and decoded by both its own interface and a foreign robot's interface. Native reconstruction anchors each robot to its demonstrated commands. Cross-robot geometric supervision trains the foreign decoder to realize the source tool target, using a positive reachability check to select admissible targets. A visual--language policy subsequently learns the shared action coordinates and executes through the appropriate native decoder. Geometry establishes a relation among action realizations. The policy must still learn from observations and language when to approach, grasp, transport and release, and closed-loop execution determines whether those decisions complete the task. Supervision connects missing robot--task edges through action realization. A source demonstration supplies the skill's tool targets. A foreign robot supplies its kinematics and native demonstrations of other skills. Together, they train its interface to realize the source tool targets without a paired joint trajectory. Native reconstruction alone leaves this cross-interface relation unspecified. Matched-exposure controls test whether learning the relation improves closed-loop execution on missing combinations. Our contributions are twofold. First, we learn heterogeneous whole-arm action interfaces from demonstration-derived tool targets. A source command supervises a foreign native decoder on reachable targets, while native reconstruction anchors demonstrated configurations. An interface-level ambiguity analysis explains why native reconstruction alone leaves foreign action semantics underspecified. Second, we supervise policy predictions through source and eligible foreign realizations using the same demonstration-derived tool targets. summary: Transverse feedback linearization (TFL) achieves path following by exactly linearizing the error dynamics, but its controller is undefined on a singular set, such as zero speed for a unicycle or zero thrust for a quadrotor. The constrained region of attraction, the set of initial states from which the closed loop converges to the path without violating state or regularity constraints, determines where the controller can be safely activated. Exploiting the exact linear error dynamics, we show that this region is the largest forward invariant subset of the admissible set. We then decompose its state-constrained Zubov value function into an analytically known quadratic cost-to-go and a safety value function. We learn only the latter, by fitted value iteration without infinite-horizon trajectory labels. The resulting estimate combines an inner layer verified by interval branch and bound with a learned outer layer tested on samples. On a unicycle following a circle and a sinusoid and on a planar quadrotor, it covers on average 72.0%, 83.4% and 19.1% of the simulated region of attraction. In comparison, the quadratic cost-to-go and two physics-informed neural network (PINN) solvers of Zubov's equation cover at most 11.3%, 4.0% and 0.0% on average. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/roa_tfl

Transverse feedback linearization (TFL) addresses both with a coordinate transformation and a feedback that inverts a decoupling matrix nielsen2006,nielsen2008,akhtar2011 . The dynamics transverse to the path then become linear and exponentially stable, while the tangential and internal dynamics govern the motion along the path. TFL controllers have been designed for unicycles nielsen2004 , car-like robots and cars with trailers akhtar2011,akhtar2015,akhtar2011thesis , quadrotors with and without a payload or a failed rotor roza2012,akhtar2012,akhtar2013,akhtar2022,akhtar2023,allawati2026,allawati2026ftc , and robotic arms, also when carried by a quadrotor hladio2013,tariq2026 . -1 In many of these works, the decoupling matrix and the Jacobian of the coordinate transformation are shown to be nonsingular on the path following manifold. By continuity and the inverse function theorem, they remain nonsingular on a neighbourhood of it, so the convergence guarantees are local nielsen2008,akhtar2015 . Beyond this neighbourhood, the domain of validity of TFL is limited by topological obstructions to globally regular path-following coordinates for closed paths. It is also limited by system-dependent singularities of the decoupling matrix, such as zero speed for the dynamically extended unicycle and zero thrust for the quadrotor nielsen2006,akhtar2015,allawati2026 . Consequently, a trajectory that starts far from the path may reach these singularities even though its transverse error decays exponentially while the controller is defined. We therefore seek the constrained region of attraction, that is, the set of initial states from which the closed-loop trajectories converge to the path while the controller remains well defined and all state constraints hold for all future time. -1 The Zubov value function characterizes regions of attraction camilli2001 , and with an obstacle term for the state constraints it is finite precisely on the constrained region of attraction gruene2015 . The difficulty is computing it. Grid-based solvers of the associated Hamilton-Jacobi equation suffer from the curse of dimensionality mitchell2005 , and sum-of-squares methods xue2020 require polynomial dynamics, whereas TFL closed loops are rational, trigonometric and singular. Neural solvers of Zubov equations treat equilibria or, in discrete time, compact invariant sets liu2025,kang2023,mengliu2026,serry2025,serry2026,meng2024 . Most are trained on labels from trajectories simulated until convergence, and none handles a path-following target set together with controller singularities. On the TFL closed loops of this paper, we measure coverage against the region of attraction found by simulating a set of reference states, which we call the simulated region of attraction (Section~ sec:exp ). Two such solvers liu2025,mengliu2026 , both physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), cover on average at most 11.3\, , 4.0\, and 0.0\, of it. To the best of our knowledge, no existing method learns the region of attraction of a TFL closed loop. The closest works on feedback linearization and path following oishi2006,faulwasser2016 do not estimate it for a given controller (Appendix~ app:related ). -1 Our key observation is that existing Zubov solvers do not exploit the exact linear error dynamics of TFL. On the admissible set, where the controller is well defined, the coordinate transformation is regular and the state constraints hold, these dynamics make the constrained region of attraction the largest forward invariant subset. As a result, only the safety value function has to be learned, from short trajectory segments and without infinite-horizon trajectory labels. title: Lyapunov-Inspired Sustained Balance on Dynamically Responsive Supports
summary: Conventional balance formulations often assume a rigid, stationary support, decoupling body stabilization from support motion. This assumption becomes inadequate on mechanically responsive supports, creating a coupled control challenge: corrective body motions intended to restore equilibrium can also excite support motion. We formulate sustained balance as a coupled regulation problem that coordinates equilibrium restoration with suppression of motion induced by the robot's own corrections. We introduce LISST (Lyapunov-Inspired Sustained Stabilization), a learning framework that accounts for how earlier actions shape the conditions for subsequent corrections. It uses recent observations to support immediate adjustments and longer histories to characterize persistent motion, with physical supervision relating the learned representation to robot-support behavior. To evaluate corrective actions, LISST uses coupled dynamics to assess both imbalance and the direction of motion. A Lyapunov-inspired criterion measures progress over finite windows, accommodating the transients required to restore balance. This physical evaluation guides joint-level policy learning through backpropagation through differentiable model rollouts. Privileged guidance focuses training on difficult states reached by the deployment policy and is transferred through distillation. The resulting policy operates using only onboard proprioception. Real-world experiments demonstrate that LISST maintains balance while limiting residual oscillations during continuous interaction with a dynamically responsive support. Video: youtu.be/iGHU7S4wPyw.

This physical evaluation guides joint-level policy learning through backpropagation through differentiable model rollouts. Privileged guidance focuses training on difficult states reached by the deployment policy and is transferred through distillation. The resulting policy operates using only onboard proprioception. Introduction sec:introduction alancing on a mechanically responsive support requires corrective movements that also alter the supporting surface. Whole-body controllers coordinate body motion and contact forces~ sentis2010compliant,righetti2013optimal , which also affect the support~ nava2017modeling . Shifting the robot can restore static moment balance, while the acceleration and braking needed to reach that configuration can excite support motion. The resulting robot--support motion can persist after the static imbalance has been compensated. Each subsequent correction therefore begins with the motion left by earlier actions. We study sustained balance as the continuous regulation of coupled robot--support motion to establish and maintain equilibrium. We investigate this problem with a quadruped on a passive, pitch-hinged board under changing endpoint loads, preserving physical state and controller history throughout the interaction. The robot chooses body and contact adjustments without a prescribed reference motion, using onboard proprioception at deployment. Output-feedback controllers stabilize simplified robots on unstable supports without direct environmental feedback~ nagarajan2014balancing , while coupled robot--support models describe and control their shared dynamics~ nava2017modeling . For quadrupeds on moving platforms, LAS-MP combines adaptive postural control with proprioceptive robot and platform state estimation~ yoon2024lasmp . In sustained balance, each correction begins with the motion left by earlier actions, which can change whether the next movement suppresses or amplifies the response. A proprioceptive policy therefore needs information about this ongoing response and an action evaluation that accounts for it. We introduce LISST (Lyapunov-Inspired Sustained Stabilization), a learning framework that uses interaction history to inform corrective actions. Similar body postures can occur during quiet balance or at an oscillation turning point, so posture alone does not identify the ongoing response. History-based locomotion and adaptation use past observations to infer control context~ lee2020learning,kumar2021rma . For sustained balance, longer histories characterize persistent motion, while recent observations support immediate adjustments. Interpreting motion also requires a criterion for whether a correction advances balance. Equal relative kinetic energy can correspond to motion toward or away from equilibrium, and the acceleration required for correction acts back on the support. LISST uses coupled dynamics to evaluate these directional effects and a Lyapunov-inspired criterion to assess progress over finite windows, allowing for corrective transients. This physical evaluation guides the joint-target policy through backpropagation through time (BPTT) in differentiable world-model rollouts~ fussell2021supertrack,hafner2020dreamer , connecting the simplified dynamics to the actual action interface. Training must also account for the difficult states created by the deployment policy's own corrections. LISST directs privileged guidance to these states, preserving their accumulated motion and observation history, and transfers it through context distillation. The deployed policy requires only proprioception. Our main contributions are as follows: Structured Temporal Representation-Based Control. We develop a policy that uses short-history context and supervised joint/body estimates for immediate adjustments, together with a structured temporal representation of ongoing motion. Learned signals are parameterized by offset, amplitude, frequency, and phase and related to robot--support motion through physical reconstruction and short-term continuation. These complementary inputs let the Actor condition corrective actions on both the current body state and the evolving motion pattern. Physics-Informed Lyapunov-Inspired Optimization. Coupled dynamics guide policy optimization by evaluating imbalance together with the direction of relative motion. A load-aware finite-window Lyapunov-inspired decay criterion accommodates corrective transients, and BPTT through differentiable world-model rollouts carries this physical evaluation to the joint-target policy. The analysis relates realized window decrease to conditional convergence and boundedness. Residual-Guided Privileged Policy Learning. Bounded residual corrections to the deployment context provide privileged guidance through a shared Actor. Some privileged rollouts start from low-value and pre-failure states encountered by the deployment policy, preserving physical state, load context, observation history, and reward memory. Distillation on states collected by the deployment policy transfers this guidance to the situations arising from the policy's own interaction with the support. Related Work sec:related Dynamic Balance and Robot--Environment Interaction Model-based balance control coordinates whole-body motion with contact forces and support constraints. Sentis et al.~ sentis2010compliant regulate center-of-mass behavior and internal forces, while Righetti et al.~ righetti2013optimal optimize contact-force distribution through inverse dynamics. Capturability analysis relates stopping without falling to foot placement, support geometry, and angular momentum~ koolen2012capturability . Trajectory optimization and model predictive control account for contact interactions over finite horizons~ posa2014direct,dicarlo2018dynamic . Moving supports introduce additional dynamics. Lee and Goswami~ lee2012momentum regulate momentum on nonstationary ground, while Gao et al.~ gao2025swaying use time-varying foot-placement control for walking on swaying surfaces. Nagarajan and Yamane~ nagarajan2014balancing stabilize simplified planar robots on unstable supports without direct environmental feedback. Nava et al.~ nava2017modeling model robot--seesaw dynamics and contact constraints and demonstrate coupled stabilization in simulation. LAS-MP~ yoon2024lasmp learns adaptive postural control with proprioceptive robot and platform state estimation. These studies motivate treating the support as part of the dynamics. Our focus is the continuing response to corrective actions, including the motion that remains after static compensation. Learning-Based Legged Locomotion and Adaptation Reinforcement learning enables quadrupeds to acquire motor skills in simulation and transfer them to physical robots~ hwangbo2019learning . The information available to the policy shapes its ability to adapt: Lee et al.~ lee2020learning use proprioceptive history for locomotion on challenging terrain, whereas Miki et al.~ miki2022learning combine proprioceptive and exteroceptive feedback. RMA~ kumar2021rma infers an adaptation context from recent observations and actions, and Margolis et al.~ margolis2024rapid combine a command curriculum with online system identification. Privileged learning transfers simulation information to policies with restricted deployment inputs~ lee2020learning,kumar2021rma . The states on which guidance is provided also matter. DAgger~ ross2011dagger addresses the expert--learner state-distribution mismatch through supervision on learner-visited states. Beyond the information and guidance available to a policy, learning depends on how its actions are evaluated. Learned world models predict action-conditioned transitions for planning or policy improvement through imagined trajectories~ hafner2019latent,hafner2025worldmodels . Physical structure can guide how those trajectories are evaluated. CLF-RL~ li2026clfrl constructs tracking and Lyapunov-decay rewards from model-generated reference motions, and finite-step control Lyapunov methods assess decrease over multiple transitions~ noroozi2019finitestep . Our objective addresses load compensation without a prescribed reference motion. It uses the physical model to evaluate signed corrective motion jointly with imbalance and support motion, retaining the reaction of acceleration on the support. State Estimation and Motion Representation State estimation recovers feedback variables from sensor measurements. Bloesch et al.~ bloesch2012state fuse leg kinematics and inertial measurements, while Hartley et al.~ hartley2020contact use contact-aided invariant filtering to estimate pose, velocity, and contact points. Camurri et al.~ camurri2017probabilistic estimate contact reliability and detect impacts. On moving ground, He et al.~ he2026noninertial estimate robot state relative to noninertial ground using encoders and IMUs on both the robot and support. Temporal encoders and adaptation modules extract control context from interaction history~ lee2020learning,kumar2021rma , while DreamWaQ~ nahrendra2023dreamwaq learns implicit terrain information from proprioception. DeepPhase~ starke2022deepphase learns periodic embeddings of full-body motion, and Fourier Latent Dynamics~ li2024fld uses a predictive Fourier representation for motion encoding and generation. For sustained balance, the representation must describe the motion already in progress when the next correction begins. This motivates relating latent temporal coordinates to robot--support motion through physical supervision. We next formulate the coupled mechanics and the proprioceptive control interface on which LISST operates. Problem Formulation sec:problem Task and State Description We consider a quadruped on a rigid board that rotates passively about a fixed pitch hinge at . The robot shifts its body and relocates its feet to compensate changing endpoint loads, without a prescribed reference motion or balancing location. Load updates preserve the mechanical state and controller history throughout each continuous episode. For a fixed load with feasible balance, the target is a level, stationary board, zero net static torque, and vanishing robot motion relative to the board while maintaining support. The robot configuration satisfying these conditions can vary with the load.

title: Pelorus: Resource-Aware Lidar-Inertial Odometry
summary: Lidar-inertial odometry (LIO) has an efficiency problem. High-resolution lidars produce millions of points per second that must be processed online on the resource-constrained hardware of robots, cars, or drones, yet most LIO methods neither bound their memory nor report their compute footprint. We introduce Pelorus, a resource-aware LIO with a fixed-capacity multiresolution map of voxelized normal distributions and an iterated equivariant state estimator. A relevance-based eviction keeps the map memory bounded, and a maturity-weighted map update suppresses inconsistent observations. The pipeline runs in parallel on CPUs and GPUs. On five sequences from three public datasets, Pelorus achieves the lowest relative pose error in seven of ten metrics with a small, bounded memory footprint and, with GPU offloading, the lowest CPU load of all compared methods. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, it processes a 128-beam lidar at 10 Hz. Pelorus is open source with CUDA, Vulkan, and Metal backends.
full_text: Pelorus: Resource-Aware Lidar-Inertial Odometry Charlotte Sieh\, and Mario Porrmann\, Sieh and Porrmann: Pelorus: Resource-Aware Lidar-Inertial Odometry Lidar-inertial odometry (LIO) has an efficiency problem. High-resolution lidars produce millions of points per second that must be processed online on the resource-constrained hardware of robots, cars, or drones, yet most LIO methods neither bound their memory nor report their compute footprint. We introduce Pelorus, a resource-aware LIO with a fixed-capacity multiresolution map of voxelized normal distributions and an iterated equivariant state estimator. A relevance-based eviction keeps the map memory bounded, and a maturity-weighted map update suppresses inconsistent observations. The pipeline runs in parallel on CPUs and GPUs. On five sequences from three public datasets, Pelorus achieves the lowest relative pose error in seven of ten metrics with a small, bounded memory footprint and, with GPU offloading, the lowest CPU load of all compared methods. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, it processes a 128-beam lidar at 10~Hz. Pelorus is open source with CUDA, Vulkan, and Metal backends. Embedded systems for robotic and automation, sensor fusion, SLAM Introduction Mobile robots need reliable localization in unseen environments, and depending on external infrastructure such as the Global Positioning System (GPS) is a risk for full autonomy. Lidar-inertial odometry (LIO), which fuses lidar point clouds with measurements of an inertial measurement unit (IMU), has therefore become a standard for self-contained localization and the frontend of many simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) systems. Since LIO runs on the mobile platform next to the tasks that rely on it, resource efficiency is a strict requirement. A method whose memory grows with the trajectory eventually fails, which restricts it to bounded offline use. An odometry also has to leave room for other software by keeping a small and predictable computational footprint. While related work shows promising accuracy, the hardware resources needed for these results are rarely reported. At the same time, embedded boards with a low power consumption increasingly feature general-purpose GPUs. Offloading LIO to these GPUs can significantly reduce its CPU footprint, but existing methods do not target these hardware limits. This work introduces Pelorus, a resource-aware LIO that achieves state-of-the-art relative accuracy within a bounded local map ( ) and scales down to an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, processing high-resolution scans at sensor rate. Pelorus' main contributions are listed as follows: A fixed-capacity multiresolution local map of voxelized normal distributions with a relevance-based eviction score and a maturity-weighted update, which bounds memory independent of trajectory length while suppressing inconsistent observations. A resource-aware LIO pipeline using preallocated buffers and data structures suited to single-instruction, multiple-thread (SIMT) execution to run at sensor rate on an embedded GPU. A permissive open-source implementation with CUDA, Vulkan, and Metal backends, distributed as libraries, framework integrations, and standalone binaries. Related Work Lidar-inertial odometry has to process millions of points per second online on the hardware of the platform it localizes. The memory of the local map must not grow with the trajectory for continuous operation, and the compute per scan must fit the sensor period on embedded processors while leaving room for the software that relies on the odometry. We review LIO methods along these two constraints. Early methods like LOAM by Zhang and Singh~ loam and F-LOAM by Wang~et~al.~ floam reduce the compute by extracting edge and plane features before the registration, at the cost of assumptions on the scene. LOAM uses the IMU only for initial guesses and deskewing, which is known as loosely coupled LIO, while F-LOAM works without an IMU. LIO-SAM by Shan~et~al.~ liosam couples IMU preintegration and lidar odometry factors in a factor graph that also estimates the IMU biases, a tightly coupled formulation. The graph optimization is sequential which weighs on the ARM cores of embedded boards. Koide~et~al.~ gicpgpu,glim evaluate generalized iterative closest point (GICP) matching cost factors on the GPU, but the odometry of GLIM still bounds the optimization by a fixed-lag window of keyframes. Filter-based methods avoid this cost by correcting the navigation state directly with the lidar measurements, so their resource use is dominated by the local map. FAST-LIO2 by Xu~et~al.~ fastlio2 uses an iterated Kalman filter on manifolds~ ikfom and registers the scan points against an incremental kd-tree that is trimmed to a box around the sensor. Its memory is thus bounded by volume and depends on the point density, and rebuilding parts of the tree interrupts the otherwise per-point parallel neighbor search. Point-LIO by He~et~al.~ pointlio keeps this map and fuses every point individually into the filter state for robustness under highly dynamic motion. Faster-LIO by Bai~et~al.~ fasterlio replaces the tree with incremental voxels (iVox), a voxel hashmap that parallelizes neighbor search and map update and bounds the number of voxels with a least-recently-used (LRU) cache. Recency is a simple retention criterion, but it does not distinguish well-observed geometry from a few recent returns. DLIO by Chen~et~al.~ dlio instead registers the scan with GICP against a submap of keyframes after continuous-time motion correction. Since the keyframes are retained, its memory grows with the explored area. The Equivariant Filter (EqF) by van Goor~et~al.~ eqf,eqftac further evolves the state estimation model. It defines the estimation error through system symmetries, which reduces linearization errors. Tao~et~al.~ eqlio apply it to LIO in Eq-LIO, coupling navigation, IMU biases, and lidar--IMU extrinsics through a semidirect product symmetry with gravity constrained on the two-dimensional sphere. Instead of storing points, a map can summarize each voxel by a distribution. This compresses the local geometry into a fixed size per voxel and lets every voxel be fitted and matched independently, which suits parallel hardware. The Normal Distributions Transform (NDT)~ ndtbiber fits a Gaussian per voxel. LiTAMIN by Yokozuka~et~al.~ litamin stabilizes NDT-based lidar odometry with a regularized covariance, and S-NDT by Renaut~et~al.~ smoothndt smooths the NDT map to widen the convergence basin. To reduce the computational load, Sun~et~al.~ lightweightlio combine NDT matching with IMU-based deskewing, and Ren~et~al.~ odomfeat extract plane and edge features before the NDT matching. iG-LIO by Chen~et~al.~ chen2024iglio tightly couples GICP with the IMU on an LRU-bounded voxel map like iVox and estimates a covariance for every scan point from neighboring voxels, so covariances are computed for both the map and the scan. FAR-LIO by Leitenstern~et~al.~ farlio accelerates a sparsity-aware GICP on a GPU voxel hashmap for autonomous racing and fuses it with the IMU in an extended Kalman filter with a kinematic motion model. These works reduce the cost per scan but mainly focus on runtime speed. Uneven spatial sampling further motivates several map resolutions. MARS by Quenzel and Behnke~ mars combines multiresolution surfel maps with continuous-time registration and bounds each level by an egocentric volume and a keyframe window. VoxelMap by Yuan~et~al.~ voxelmap refines voxels in octrees according to the local planarity and keeps a global map. Pelorus adopts a multiresolution map of distributions, but bounds the number of distributions per level instead of the covered volume and selects the ones to keep by their relevance. Hardware acceleration on embedded systems is a further strategy, for example truncated signed distance field (TSDF) mapping accelerated on a field-programmable gate array (FPGA)~ hatsdf , a heterogeneous FPGA and GPU SLAM for drones~ redrose , and FeatSense by Gaal~et~al.~ featsense , which runs feature-based odometry on the CPU and TSDF mapping on the GPU of Jetson boards. These systems lower the compute per scan, but their dense maps remain hard to bound in memory~ featsense,redrose . In summary, existing LIO methods bound their local map by volume, by recency, or by a keyframe window, or not at all, and the methods that accelerate LIO on embedded hardware target the compute per scan. The resources the methods need on such hardware are rarely reported. To our knowledge, no LIO combines a tightly coupled filter with a map of distributions, retained by relevance, in a pipeline that processes high-resolution scans at sensor rate on an embedded GPU with a measured resource footprint. Pelorus addresses this combination. Method We call an odometry resource-aware if its memory and compute footprints are bounded, small, and predictable, so it can run alongside the application that relies on it. Every step of Pelorus is therefore designed GPU-first with a focus on parallelization, cache locality, preallocation, and avoids data structures that grow with the input size. Preprocessing Vendor-specific input points are converted on the fly to a standardized point type by a per-point abstraction passed through the pipeline, which saves a temporary cloud buffer and a separate conversion pass. Every buffer, including scratch buffers for matrix operations, is sized by the scan and allocated once at initialization, so the pipeline does not allocate memory over time and keeps its accesses cache-local. The first preprocessing step removes invalid measurements, such as returns from the platform itself, and downsamples the scan to harmonize the point density. Preprocessing runs sequentially or in parallel on the CPU, or on a GPU backend, where it requires an additional copy of the incoming cloud. The IMU timestamps are then used to predict the state of an equivariant filter following Eq-LIO~ eqlio . The predictions are computed sequentially, stored, and used to deskew the scan in parallel. title: CoSphere-SLAM: Multi-Agent Panoramic Gaussian Splatting SLAM with Spherical Loop Closure

summary: Dense collaborative mapping is essential for search and rescue, building inspection, and warehouse automation, where panoramic cameras capture the entire surroundings in a single frame. Unlike pinhole agents that share views only at similar headings, panoramic agents observe overlapping scenes at any 3D orientation, yet searching full rotations also produces mutually consistent false loop closures across distinct symmetric rooms. Moreover, continuous monocular scale drift splits rigidly merged maps at revisited surfaces, while depth noise at short baselines distorts loop translation directions. To address these challenges, we propose CoSphere-SLAM, the first multi-agent Gaussian splatting SLAM framework for panoramic cameras, whose spherical loop closure aligns spherical features over $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ via fast Fourier correlation across arbitrary orientations and rejects symmetric false closures through global $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ consensus. Building on these closures, directional global optimization solves a per-keyframe $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ pose graph with log-scale regularization to correct scale drift while separating optical-flow translation directions from depth-based magnitudes. Finally, omnidirectional Gaussian fusion transforms each Gaussian with its keyframe similarity and renders Gaussians at their maximum ray response to jointly refine poses and maps. Experiments on indoor and cross-session multi-agent panoramic benchmarks demonstrate that CoSphere-SLAM achieves state-of-the-art trajectory accuracy and rendering quality among single-agent and multi-agent methods. Project website: https://cosphere-slam.github.io.

Introduction Dense 3D mapping of large indoor environments is essential for search and rescue, building inspection, and warehouse automation, where 3D Gaussian splatting kerbl20233dgs enables dense photorealistic SLAM from a moving camera keetha2024splatam,matsuki2024monogs,huang2024photoslam . Equipping an agent with a panoramic camera is particularly effective indoors, since each frame captures the whole room in one pass and constrains motion in all directions lee2024odgs,li2025omnigs,mao2026panogsslam,guo2026cubesplat,spiss2026odgsslam . Even with views, however, a single agent observes the scene along only one path, where walls and furniture occlude surfaces behind them, visiting rooms one by one is slow, and monocular scale and pose drift accumulate across rooms. Mapping large indoor spaces rapidly and completely therefore requires extending single-agent panoramic SLAM to multiple agents exploring parallel routes and sessions schmuck2019ccm,lajoie2020door,tian2022kimera . Yet existing multi-agent systems hu2023cpslam,deng2024mne,yugay2025magic,xu2025macego3d,mags2025,como3r rely on narrow pinhole views and RGB-D inputs or rigid submaps, missing meetings across different headings on cropped views while failing under equirectangular distortion, symmetric rooms, and scale drift on panoramas. Extending panoramic Gaussian SLAM to multiple agents must resolve three coupled challenges across loop closure, global optimization, and map fusion. First, as mobile cameras pitch and roll across arbitrary headings, yaw shifts an equirectangular image cyclically along longitude, whereas tilt warps rows differently across latitudes and breaks planar matching. Moreover, searching full 3D rotations matches symmetric rooms up to a rigid transform, and unlike random outliers, all matches in a symmetric layout imply the same wrong transform between agents, so pairwise robust kernels cannot reject them. Second, monocular trajectories drift continuously in scale between distant meetings, whereas depth errors at short baselines shift 3D point alignment in proportion to scene depth and corrupt translation directions. Third, varying scale corrections split rigidly merged submaps at revisited walls, while projecting 3D Gaussians onto a tangent plane stretches them near the poles and cuts across the seam. A monocular panorama observes the unit sphere without field-of-view limits, providing scale-free viewing directions while leaving discrete room symmetries and continuous radial scale unobservable. Whereas search turns symmetric rooms into coherent outlier clusters and isotropic alignment conflates flow directions with depth noise, CoSphere-SLAM couples three designs to resolve both ambiguities without distortion (Figure~ fig:teaser ). Building on per-agent full-sphere tracking and ray-based mapping, spherical loop closure correlates features over at arbitrary orientations and enforces cycle-consistent global consensus across agent loops to reject symmetric clusters. Directional global optimization then solves an anisotropic per-keyframe pose graph separating flow directions from scale drift, and omnidirectional Gaussian fusion deforms Gaussians by keyframe similarities to refine poses and maps along viewing rays. Our main contributions are as follows: 1pt 0pt 2pt We design the first multi-agent panoramic Gaussian splatting SLAM framework, CoSphere-SLAM, unifying full-sphere camera tracking, compact descriptor communication, and dense mapping without prior poses or scales. We propose spherical loop closure to correlate features over at arbitrary orientations and reject symmetric false closures via global consensus. We introduce directional global optimization to separate optical-flow translation directions from monocular scale drift on a per-keyframe pose graph. We develop omnidirectional Gaussian fusion to align local Gaussians with per-keyframe similarities and jointly refine poses and maps along viewing rays. Related Work sec:related -Agent SLAM. Collaborative SLAM merges agent trajectories through inter-agent loop closures. Centralized systems schmuck2019ccm,schmuck2021covins optimize a global map on a server, whereas distributed systems lajoie2020door,tian2022kimera,lajoie2024swarm exchange compact descriptors and solve the pose graph across agents. To reject false inter-agent closures, these systems use pairwise consistency maximization mangelson2018pcm , graduated non-convexity yang2020gnc , and robust kernels such as dynamic covariance scaling agarwal2013dcs , while cycle consistency over pose loops resolves symmetric structures in structure from motion zach2010disambiguating . However, pairwise kernels reject only mutually inconsistent outliers, and pinhole views connect agents only at similar headings. Collaborative Mapping. Beyond single-agent Gaussian splatting SLAM, feed-forward models now reconstruct long monocular sequences deng2025vggtlong,chen2026ttt3r . For multiple agents, CP-SLAM hu2023cpslam shares neural point clouds between two agents, MNE-SLAM deng2024mne distributes a neural implicit map, and MAGiC-SLAM yugay2025magic and MAC-Ego3D xu2025macego3d merge Gaussian splatting maps of RGB-D agents. MAGS-SLAM mags2025 extends Gaussian splatting to monocular agents with submap-level alignment, and CoMo3R-SLAM como3r builds dense multi-agent maps with 3D reconstruction priors. All of them, however, rely on pinhole images and connect agents only where narrow views overlap, whereas panoramas share content whenever paths pass nearby. SLAM and Reconstruction. Panoramic cameras observe the full sphere and therefore constrain camera motion in all directions. OpenVSLAM sumikura2019openvslam and 360VO huang2022360vo track equirectangular images with sparse features and direct alignment, while omnidirectional Gaussian splatting reconstructs scenes from posed or unposed panoramas lee2024odgs,li2025omnigs,zhuang2026pfgs360 and extends to single-agent panoramic video SLAM mao2026panogsslam,guo2026cubesplat,spiss2026odgsslam . In multi-robot estimation, Omni-swarm xu2022omniswarm and D SLAM xu2024d2slam use omnidirectional cameras in aerial swarms, yet estimate only sparse states without loop closure, scale correction, or dense mapping. While each panorama observes the full sphere of viewing directions, monocular scale and room symmetry remain unobservable within one view. Introduction sec:intro Aerial vision--language navigation (VLN) enables unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow natural-language instructions using visual observations~ wang2025uavflow,Fan_2026_CVPR . By expressing goals through objects, spatial relations and motion commands, users can specify flight tasks without constructing detailed waypoint sequences. This capability supports intuitive human--robot interaction and flexible autonomous navigation in complex environments. Reliable aerial VLN requires the vehicle to ground language in continuous three-dimensional motion, track the progress of multi-stage tasks, and avoid obstacles throughout execution. Recent world--action models couple visual representations with action generation~ yuan2026fastwam , providing a foundation for aerial policies such as WorldVLN and WorldFly~ worldvln2026,worldfly2026 . Turning these predictions into complete flights brings three learning challenges. First, action policies can rely on visual shortcuts when the requested motion changes~ fang2026counterfactual , making language-responsive control essential. Second, multi-stage instructions require persistent knowledge of completed requirements to guide subsequent actions and determine when to stop~ ma2019selfmonitor,huang2026aiep . Third, obstacle avoidance requires feedback on the path induced by predicted actions and the vehicle's motion response~ zhang2025diffphys . These challenges connect instruction grounding, execution history and physical motion within the same control loop. In this paper, we propose a world--action UAV framework that connects language response, task progress and obstacle-aware motion ( ). The action expert reads the instruction through text cross-attention and undergoes targeted post-training for instruction-responsive motion while preserving pretrained conditioning modules. A recurrent instruction-consumption head predicts completed requirements, continuously reweights the complete instruction inside the frozen executor, and supplies task-level stopping. Safety post-training in reconstructed Gaussian scenes combines successful-detour imitation with geometric feedback differentiated through vehicle tracking dynamics. Constrained adapter updates retain general-task behavior, and direct one-step denoising reduces deployment cost. title: Cross3DGS: Unified Vulkan-Based 3D Gaussian Splatting Training from Workstations to Mobile Devices
comment: Accepted to the WACV 2027 Workshop on Eyes of the Future (EOF). 19 pages including appendix
summary: Scenes captured with handheld and wearable cameras are still shipped to a CUDA workstation for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training. Training on the device that captured them, or on its companion phone or laptop, requires more than translating kernels: GPUs and drivers differ in parallel features, memory limits, and command submission, and these differences decide whether a training schedule executes and returns the correct update. We present Cross3DGS, a cross-vendor, cross-platform Vulkan trainer that keeps one optimizer and chooses its execution schedule per device in two steps: rules on device limits, workload size, and observed driver failures exclude the schedules known not to run correctly, and a fixed preference order selects one of the remaining feasible schedules. The same core completes standard-quality training (30k updates, one million Gaussians) on every configuration we measured, spanning NVIDIA, Intel, Arm, Qualcomm, AMD, and Apple GPUs and including Android devices and an iPhone, whereas the existing portable trainers VkSplat and Brush do not run on some of the mobile GPUs. Averaged over 11 scenes on a workstation, Cross3DGS has higher quality than VkSplat with no significant difference in training time, and Brush reports about three times the training time at comparable quality. The final quality of Cross3DGS is nearly identical across devices. A mobile application turns a handheld capture into a viewable model entirely on the device.

Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl3dgs makes radiance-field reconstruction fast enough that the bottleneck has moved from optimization time to where optimization can run. Captures from phones, tablets, smart eyewear, and other wearable cameras are still transferred to a workstation with a CUDA GPU. Training on the capture device or its companion phone or laptop would keep private spaces on the device, remove the round trip, and work offline. We target this as batch work after a capture, for example while the phone charges: on our phones training takes minutes to hours. Commercial and research systems already move parts of this pipeline off the workstation~ scaniverse,vksplat,brush,pocketgs , but no trainer we are aware of completes standard-quality training (30k updates, up to one million Gaussians) on all eight desktop, laptop, phone, and tablet GPU configurations that we measure, which span six vendors. Writing the kernels in a cross-vendor shading language does not by itself make the trainer portable~ donaldson2017shader,decoupledfallback . Each step of 3DGS training translates to portable compute kernels, yet the execution schedule around them does not port. Subgroup width, float32 atomic add, the storage-buffer range, and the reliability of batched command submission differ across our devices, and they decide whether a nominally equivalent step completes and returns a correct update. The Vulkan trainer VkSplat~ vksplat needs subgroups of at least 32 lanes and has no mobile host, and the WebGPU trainer Brush~ brush exceeds the storage-buffer range of the GPU; of the eight configurations we measure, they complete standard-quality training on four and six (Figure~ fig:high-low-overview ). Cross3DGS therefore keeps one optimizer and a catalog of execution schedules, and chooses a schedule for each device in two steps. Step~1 excludes the schedules known not to run correctly on the device: those that exceed its limits or the workload, and those that failed on its driver. Step~2 selects one of the remaining feasible schedules with a fixed preference order. Offline tests confirm that the gradient methods in the catalog compute the same update within floating-point tolerance. title: PhyVGGT: Feed-Forward Articulated Object Reconstruction from Monocular Videos
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Project page: https://phyvggt.github.io
summary: Reconstructing an articulated object with its 3D movable parts, joint parameters and unseen articulation states from an uncalibrated monocular video is essential for robot manipulation and interactive digital twins. Existing per-scene optimisation methods require minutes to hours and external depth or camera poses, whereas feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct dense point maps in one pass without segmenting movable parts or inferring joints. Even on these monocular point maps, regressing or fitting continuous joints directly fails on casual videos, since cross-frame attention blurs moving part boundaries in deep layers, underestimates motion along the viewing ray and leaves continuous axes ill-conditioned under small opening angles. To address these challenges, we propose PhyVGGT, a single-pass framework on a frozen 3D foundation model that anchors moving-part matching and closed-form joint estimation to the undistorted geometry of the stationary base. First, our Part and Motion Decoder fuses intermediate per-frame tokens with global tokens and references part queries to a static-base query to segment 3D parts, align point maps on the static base and predict learned Bingham priors. Second, our Kinematic Inference Layer fits an orthogonal Manhattan frame to static surface normals, selects the joint axis in closed form under a Bingham posterior combining pairwise motion scatter with the learned priors, and solves a linear system for the hinge pivot to drive unseen states. Trained solely on synthetic data, PhyVGGT achieves state-of-the-art monocular performance across five benchmarks, outperforming FAMOS and monocular ArtiPoint, surpassing posed RGB-D ArtiPoint in median error, and running in 6.8 s per 48-frame video against hours of per-scene optimisation in Articulat3D. Introduction sec:intro Robotic manipulation and interactive simulation require reconstructing an articulated object in 3D, including its geometry, movable parts, joint types, axes, pivots and joint states. Although feed-forward 3D foundation models~ dust3r,vggt,pi3 recover dense point maps and cameras from uncalibrated images in one pass and token query heads segment static spatial relations~ relationvggt , neither models how object parts move. Conversely, per-scene optimisation methods~ paris,artgs,videoartgs,articulat3d fit explicit motion models to multi-state scans or videos, yet require minutes to hours per object alongside sensor depth, camera poses or known kinematic trees. While recent feed-forward articulation predictors~ artsplat,famos,sim2art avoid per-scene fitting, they regress unconstrained joint vectors or fit continuous displacements directly in 3D, where monocular depth errors corrupt the recovered axis and pivot. Attaching a prediction head or motion fitter directly to a frozen 3D foundation model fails on casual videos because alternating intra- and cross-frame attention~ vggt treats the scene as static. In deep global-attention layers, moving part edges blur into the stationary body and camera drift mixes with part motion, while cross-frame context biases moving-part depth towards other frames and underestimates displacement along the viewing ray. When the canonical rest pose is also unknown, Fisher information for continuous axis and pivot estimation vanishes quadratically under small opening angles~ woltring1985 , leaving unconstrained regression and motion fitting ill-conditioned. Unlike moving parts, the stationary base is unaffected by cross-frame depth bias and remains geometrically accurate across frames. In manufactured cabinets, appliances and furniture, flat faces meet at right angles, so revolute and prismatic axes align with the three orthogonal directions of the static base's Manhattan frame~ straub2014mixture while hinge pivots lie along the boundary between the part and the base. Benefiting from this undistorted anchor, we redesign both feature decoding and joint inference around the stationary base. Referencing part queries to the static base cancels camera drift during dense matching, and restricting candidate axes to the static Manhattan frame turns ill-conditioned continuous regression into closed-form three-way selection that tolerates up to of tilt towards the viewing ray. Based on this design, we propose PhyVGGT, a single-pass framework on a frozen visual geometry model~ vggt that reconstructs 3D movable parts, joint parameters and unseen articulation states from an uncalibrated monocular video, as shown in Figure~ fig:teaser . First, our Part and Motion Decoder introduces multi-layer per-frame and global token fusion together with an explicit static-base query, recovering sharp 3D part masks, correspondences aligned to the static base and learned Bingham priors. Second, our Kinematic Inference Layer fits an orthogonal Manhattan frame to static surface normals via fourth-order alignment, selects the joint axis in closed form under a Bingham posterior~ bingham1974 combining pairwise motion scatter with the learned priors, and solves a positive-definite linear system for the hinge pivot to drive unseen states. Our contributions are as follows: We introduce PhyVGGT, a single-pass framework on a frozen 3D model that anchors part matching and closed-form joint estimation to the stationary base to reconstruct 3D parts, joints and unseen states from a monocular video. We propose a Part and Motion Decoder that fuses multi-layer per-frame and global tokens and references part queries to a static-base query to recover sharp 3D part masks and correspondences aligned on the static base. We design a Kinematic Inference Layer that restricts joint estimation to the Manhattan frame of the static base, removing depth bias along the viewing ray through closed-form Bingham axis selection and linear hinge pivot estimation. Related Work sec:related Articulated Object Reconstruction Early learning methods predict part coordinates and joint parameters from depth scans~ ancsh,screwnet , whereas per-scene optimisation fits neural radiance fields or 3D Gaussians to discrete articulation states~ paris,artgs or continuous videos~ videoartgs,articulat3d . Articulation in Prime~ aip shortens per-object fitting to roughly ten minutes, yet still requires external depth maps, camera poses and part masks. Casual and egocentric pipelines likewise depend on RGB-D input~ itaco : ArtiPoint~ artipoint fits joints to tracked 3D interaction points under known odometry, MoMa-SG~ momasg constructs articulated scene graphs from RGB-D sequences, and PAWS~ paws lifts 2D hand trajectories with sensor depth and poses before querying a vision-language model over surface candidates. Avoiding per-scene optimisation and depth sensors, single-image predictors infer openable parts from appearance priors~ opdmulti,monoart,urdfanything,articulateanything , ArtSplat~ artsplat and FAMOS~ famos predict joints from multi-state point clouds, and sim2art~ sim2art estimates part masks and continuous joint vectors from monocular videos. Yet predicting unconstrained vectors in or fitting continuous axes directly to monocular point maps propagates depth errors along the viewing ray into the joint estimate, whereas PhyVGGT anchors part matching and closed-form Bingham inference to the Manhattan frame of the static base in one RGB pass. Feed-Forward 3D Foundation Models DUSt3R~ dust3r and MASt3R~ mast3r predict dense 3D point maps from uncalibrated image pairs in a shared coordinate frame, while VGGT~ vggt and ~ pi3 recover point maps, camera poses and point tracks across an entire video in one forward pass. summary: Recent world action models (WAMs) drop future prediction at inference, assuming that representations learned through auxiliary future supervision still benefit action generation. However, our layerwise analysis of Fast-WAM reveals a depth-dependent mismatch: while probes decode future state transitions more accurately from deeper visual layers, the gradients and visual focuses of the future and action objectives increasingly diverge with depth, leaving much of this predictive information unused by the action pathway. To address this issue, we introduce RelayWAM, which adds an explicit transition space between the video and action backbones. Conditioned on the task instruction, robot state, and current action estimate, recurrent transition layers extract step-relevant predictive cues across depth and relay them directly into the action attention, without generating future frames at inference. Experiments show that RelayWAM substantially amplifies the benefit of future supervision, translating into stronger generalization under distribution shifts in both simulation and real-world robot tasks. On LIBERO-Plus, RelayWAM achieves 72.03% mean success, compared to 56.42% without future supervision and 51.50% for Fast-WAM.

Introduction sec:intro World action models (WAMs) bring future prediction into action learning. Built on large-scale pretrained video models, they jointly learn to generate actions and to predict future observations~ motus,cosmospolicy,lingbotva,videovla,dreamzero,gr1,vpp,uwm,uva,genieenvisioner,gigaworldpolicy,nativevap,trajwam . Recent work goes further: future-prediction supervision improves policy performance even when the future-generation branch is removed at inference, and future prediction serves only as an auxiliary training objective~ fastwam,flare,vlajepa,jepawam,lightwam . The intuition is straightforward. A model that can predict ``what happens next'' should encode object dynamics and future state changes, and this should help action generation generalize. This intuition, however, rests on an implicit assumption. In Fast-WAM~ fastwam and similar models, future supervision can improve action generation through the shared representation. This design assumes that the action pathway actually uses the information that future supervision writes into this representation. Existing methods are validated mainly by success rates in simulation and on real robots. These results show that future supervision helps, but not how the representations it shapes are used. This leaves an open question: Question. What representations does future supervision shape, and are they actually used by action generation? To answer this question, we analyze future-supervised WAMs from two sides, writing and reading. On the writing side, we introduce training-focus attribution, which reveals the visual content that each objective actually relies on. We find that the two objectives are only partly aligned. Future information is indeed written into deeper layers, while the gradients of the two objectives become less aligned and their training-focus maps gradually drift apart. On the reading side, we erase this information from the features read by the action pathway. The resulting action change is close to that caused by erasing random directions of the same rank. These findings reveal a discrepancy between the information shaped by future supervision and the information utilized by action generation. These findings motivate us to build RelayWAM, which introduces an explicit interface to bridge the two pathways. It introduces a transition space between the intermediate-to-deep layers of the Video DiT and the Action DiT. Since the future information required for action generation varies across action steps and execution states, we condition transition tokens on the task instruction, robot state, and current action estimate. This allows the tokens to dynamically extract the future information most relevant to each action step from the future-supervised visual features, relay it across depth, and deliver it to the action pathway. With the transition space, the same future supervision becomes far more effective. In a controlled study, future supervision improves LIBERO-Plus success by 5.2 points on the base architecture, but by 15.6 points with the transition space. Fast-WAM~ fastwam likewise generates no future at inference; RelayWAM raises its LIBERO-Plus success rate from 51.50 to 72.03 . This also surpasses OpenWAM- (69.2 )~ openwam , which jointly generates future and action at inference. . Our contributions are as follows: We characterize how future supervision shapes shared representations and how the resulting information relates to action generation, providing a representation-level analysis of future-supervised WAMs. We introduce training-focus attribution, together with linear probes and causal erasure, to investigate the writing and reading behaviors of future-supervised representations. We build RelayWAM, which adds an explicit interface that converts future information into a form usable for action. It makes future supervision substantially more effective and achieves strong generalization in simulation and on real robots. Related Work sec:related Vision-language-action policies. VLA policies~ rt2,openvla,pi0,pi05,pi07,rdt,gr00t,smolvla,geminirobotics,dexvla,cotvla,spatialvla,univla,spatialforcing,vlastem,coalitionskill,dynahmrc generate actions from the current language instruction and visual observation. They are supervised mainly by robot trajectories, whose scale and diversity are far below internet-scale data, and policies trained only to predict actions tend to rely on the current visual appearance rather than on how the environment will evolve under interaction. WAMs address this by using pretrained video models as world models and adding future-prediction objectives that capture object dynamics and state transitions, which improves action generation and cross-task generalization~ unipi,wan,robodreamer,dreamgen . World action models. WAMs differ in how future information enters action generation. Explicit WAMs first generate future observations and then decode actions through an inverse dynamics model or an action head~ unipi,gen2act,vidar,videopolicy,mimicvideo,gr2,genieenvisioner,dreamzero . Implicit WAMs avoid pixel-level generation by compressing the future into latent representations or transition tokens, exploited through future prediction or joint future--action modeling~ motus,lawam,cosmospolicy,videovla,vpp,uwm,uva,worldvla,rynnvla002,dreamvla,gigaworldpolicy,nativevap,trajwam,wam4d,geosemwam,geo4dwam,pointworld . A third line keeps future prediction only as a training objective on the shared backbone and generates actions from the current observation alone~ flare,fastwam,vlajepa,lightwam,jepawam ; we refer to these as future-free inference (FFI) WAMs. FFI WAMs keep the benefits of future prediction at no extra deployment cost, but implicitly assume that the action pathway uses the predictive representations in the shared backbone. RelayWAM shows that the action reads this information only weakly and introduces transition layers that convert future-supervised representations into a form usable for action. title: Inertial Video World Models
summary: The physical world has inertia: it evolves from what already exists rather than being recreated at every instant. However, many existing video world models lack an explicit mechanism for inertial state evolution, leaving the continuity of motion and structure implicit in video prediction. During autoregressive rollouts, repeated reconstruction can accumulate errors and destabilize the predicted dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce InertialWorld, an Inertial Video World Model that makes inertia a structural prior for autoregressive prediction: existing scene evidence is carried across time rather than reconstructed at every step. Central to this formulation is Inertial Memory, which turns memory from passive predictive context into an evolving video state with two complementary views: a dense Eulerian grid preserves scene-aligned evidence, while persistent Lagrangian carriers bind local content to learned canonical coordinates. At each step, the model transports the carrier content according to action-conditioned motion, predicts the complete next video state from the transported carriers and dense grid, and uses a learned gate to combine transported and newly predicted content into the memory for the next step. Extensive experiments across multiple domains, including robot manipulation, 3D game simulation, and open-world navigation, demonstrate that InertialWorld achieves competitive autoregressive prediction performance against strong video world model baselines.
