Introduction sec:introduction Learned world models provide predictive environments for planning and control by modeling action-conditioned dynamics ha2018world,hafner2019learning,hafner2025mastering . Within this broader family, video world models instantiate learned dynamics through action-conditioned video prediction, enabling interactive simulation in games, robotic manipulation, and embodied navigation micheli2022transformers,bruce2024genie,yang2023learning,bar2025navigation . Autoregressive and diffusion-based formulations have substantially improved generation fidelity and controllability wu2024ivideogpt,alonso2024diamond,huang2025vid2world,zhu2026astra , while post-training further refines predicted rollouts wu2026rlvr,wu2026roboalign . Despite these advances, physical evolution is inertial: the world evolves from what already exists rather than being recreated at every instant. Most video world models, however, still formulate temporal evolution as repeated conditional generation, predicting persistent scene content again at every step rather than explicitly carrying it forward. Since each generated state conditions the next transition, small reconstruction errors can repeatedly re-enter the rollout and destabilize predicted motion and structure wang2017predrnn,babaeizadeh2021fitvid . A prominent line of research mitigates this limitation by augmenting video prediction with memory. Recurrent video predictors retain temporal features across prediction steps wang2017predrnn,wang2018predrnn++ , while transformer world models expose longer histories to the transition function chen2022transdreamer,wu2024ivideogpt . This additional context is particularly valuable when occlusion or accumulated generation noise makes the current frame ambiguous. Earlier features can retain identity and layout cues that are no longer directly visible but remain relevant to the next transition. Spatial and persistent memories preserve scene-aligned evidence across recurrent prediction steps wu2026video,zhou2026learning . Object-centric representations provide a complementary form of persistence by binding content to structured entities locatello2020object,kipf2021conditional , and their video extensions model the dynamics of these entities through time wu2022slotformer . Collectively, these mechanisms expose historical evidence to subsequent state transitions and improve temporal consistency, but retention alone does not specify how the retained content should evolve. When memory serves as context for a generic transition, the transition remains free to synthesize the next state without explicitly advancing the stored content. Transformation-based predictors demonstrate the value of warping observations or features jaderberg2015spatial,finn2016unsupervised , yet warping does not by itself make transport the recurrent evolution rule of persistent memory across model-predicted steps. Thus, memory determines which past evidence remains available, whereas inertia additionally specifies what persists and where it moves. This distinction motivates the central question of this work: To address this question, we introduce , an Inertial Video World Model that makes inertia a structural prior for autoregressive prediction: existing scene evidence is carried across time rather than reconstructed at every step. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:intro_overview , its central component, Inertial Memory, turns retained predictive context into an evolving video state with two complementary views: a dense Eulerian grid preserves scene-aligned evidence, while persistent Lagrangian carriers bind local content to learned canonical coordinates. At each step, the model transports the carrier content according to action-conditioned motion, predicts the complete next video state from the transported carriers and dense grid, and uses a learned gate to combine transported and newly predicted content into the memory for the next step. This carry-before-write transition establishes persistence as the default path of state evolution while preserving the capacity to model changes that transport alone cannot explain, without requiring object annotations or calibrated physical parameters. We evaluate on RT-1 robot manipulation brohan2022rt , Counter-Strike 3D game simulation huang2025vid2world , and RECON open-world navigation shah2021rapid . Across all three interactive domains, produces competitive autoregressive predictions against strong video world model baselines. Our contributions are threefold: We formulate inertial video world modeling, a state-evolution view of video world models in which existing scene evidence is inherited by default rather than repeatedly reconstructed. We introduce Inertial Memory, a hybrid Eulerian--Lagrangian video state that preserves dense scene evidence while transporting persistent regional content through action-conditioned coordinate motion before a learned gate updates the memory. We conduct extensive autoregressive prediction evaluations across robot manipulation, 3D game simulation, and open-world navigation, demonstrating competitive autoregressive prediction across all three domains against strong video world model baselines. Related Work sec:related_work World Models. Action-conditioned video prediction learns how future observations evolve under control oh2015action,finn2016unsupervised . Early approaches use stochastic, recurrent, and physics-inspired dynamics to model uncertainty and temporal dependence denton2018stochastic,wang2017predrnn,guen2020disentangling,babaeizadeh2021fitvid . Learned discrete representations van2017neural,esser2021taming enable scalable autoregressive and masked video prediction yan2021videogpt,yu2023magvit,yu2024language,wang2024omnitokenizer . These formulations support interactive simulation across games and robotics bruce2024genie,valevski2025diffusion,wu2024ivideogpt,yang2023learning, zhou2024dino,zhou2024robodreamer , while diffusion-based models provide an alternative generative backbone alonso2024diamond,huang2025vid2world . Reinforcement learning and alignment objectives further refine predicted rollouts wu2026rlvr,wu2026roboalign . In parallel, latent world models learn compact predictive states for planning and imagined policy learning hafner2019learning,hafner2020mastering,hafner2025mastering , sometimes prioritizing task-relevant dynamics over frame reconstruction schrittwieser2020mastering,hansen2024tdmpc2 . Rather than changing the video generator or its training objective, our work changes how the recurrent video state evolves by introducing transport-structured persistence that is compatible with different generative backbones. and Structured Video State. Existing memory mechanisms primarily determine what a video world model retains. Recurrent states and token histories preserve temporal context wang2017predrnn,wang2018predrnn++ ; spatial and persistent memories preserve scene-aligned content wu2026video,zhou2026learning ; and object-centric representations bind content to persistent entities burgess2019monet,greff2019multi,locatello2020object , with temporal extensions supporting tracking and prediction kipf2021conditional,wu2022slotformer,kipf2019contrastive . Relational models expose interactions between state elements battaglia2016interaction,kipf2018neural,battaglia2018relational , while Hamiltonian and graph-based simulators impose additional structure on state transitions greydanus2019hamiltonian,sanchez2020learning . These approaches enrich what persists, but they do not by themselves specify how retained content should evolve. A generic recurrent update can encode motion without requiring that motion to relocate content already in memory. title: PAIR: Bringing Household Robots into the Smart Home
summary: Household robots often need to operate appliances, and smart appliances offer both control panels and device APIs. Existing embodied AI simulation environments, however, model appliances solely as physical objects. We introduce PAIR, a smart-home simulation environment grounded in the Matter protocol~\footnote{https://csa-iot.org/all-solutions/matter/}, the industry standard for smart-home devices. PAIR provides 84 smart-device assets whose functional control panels and APIs act on a shared device state, with ambient conditions that evolve in response to both. From a survey of 1,443 requests, we construct a benchmark of 40 tasks that all require object manipulation yet remain solvable without API access, with 340 human demonstrations for policy training. Whether run alone, with a high-level planner, or with an API-enabled planner, two fine-tuned VLA policies complete none of the 120 evaluation episodes. Robots rarely get far enough to use the API: even with oracle plans and API access, over 90\% of failed rollouts stall at navigating, grasping, or operating a door. With a perfect oracle in place of the robot's body, the best planner still gets through only 57.3\% of its plan. When choosing between pressing a button and calling an API, several planners go by whether they can read the panel, not by API latency.\footnote{We will release our code and data upon publication.}

Introduction Building household robots that assist people with everyday tasks is a long-standing goal of embodied AI~ challenges_robot_home, homerobot, behavior1k . Performing these tasks often requires robots to operate household appliances by manipulating their controls, such as pressing buttons, turning knobs, and navigating touchscreens. Modern smart appliances, however, increasingly provide application programming interfaces (APIs), which allow external systems to read device states and send control commands through software~ matter,alexa,google_home . Household tasks often involve both physical actions, such as navigation and object manipulation, and appliance operations that can be performed through APIs. Therefore, household robots need to flexibly select and combine physical actions and API calls to accomplish everyday tasks efficiently. For example, the request ``Wash my shirt,'' requires a robot to physically load the shirt into the washing machine and close the door. Once the door is closed, the robot can start the cycle and monitor its progress through the API, without operating the control panel. Studying how robots execute such tasks at scale calls for a simulation environment where device states change over time and where physical actions and API calls operate on the same devices. Existing simulation environments~ libero, behavior1k, robocasa365 provide rich physics-based environments for robot manipulation, but they treat appliances as objects to be physically operated and do not consider smart-home settings, where devices report their states and accept commands through APIs. To bridge this gap, we introduce PAIR (Physical-API Integration Environment for Robots), a smart-home simulation environment that integrates physical and API-based device control. In PAIR, device states progress over time and respond to both physical actions and API calls, and running devices in turn change four ambient conditions of the home (temperature, illuminance, humidity, and air quality). We develop 84 smart-device assets, each with a functional physical interface and an API, across 14 appliance categories and four sensor categories that report these ambient conditions. Device states, commands, and operational constraints are defined according to the Matter protocol~ matter , an industry standard for smart-device interoperability. To ground evaluation in what people actually want from such a robot, we surveyed 129 participants about device-related household tasks they would delegate to a mobile manipulator capable of handling objects, operating appliances, and remotely controlling smart devices, and retained 1,443 requests from 108 participants after screening. We label each request with the skills it requires, using a taxonomy of robot skills in three categories, physical, perception, and human interaction (Table~ tab:skills_taxonomy ). More than half of the requests (58.4 ) involve checking a device's status or waiting for an event, and APIs alone could complete only 39.6 of them, while the remaining 60.4 also require the robot's physical actions or perception. From these requests, we construct a benchmark of 40 tasks that cover the skills in our taxonomy and all device categories in PAIR. Every task requires object manipulation yet can be completed without API access, so the same task can be evaluated with and without APIs and across policy architectures. Using this benchmark, we investigate how well current vision-language-action (VLA) policies handle such tasks. To adapt them to our robot and tasks, we collect 120 task-level demonstrations (three per task) and 220 demonstrations of atomic skills, all performed without API access. We then evaluate these policies alone, with a high-level planner, and with a planner that has API access, comparing task success and execution steps and analyzing how performance varies with the skills each task requires. None of the six VLA variants completes an evaluation task. API access raises device-operation success, yet with oracle plans and API access, more than 90 of the failed rollouts still stop at a navigation, pick, or door subtask. Even with oracle physical execution, the best planner reaches only 57.3 Progress, and several planners choose the API in response to panel visibility more consistently than to the stated API delay. Related Work Simulation Environments for Robotics. Simulation environments have been a cornerstone of embodied AI research, enabling scalable training and evaluation in household environments while reducing the cost of real-world experiments. Early examples such as VirtualHome~ virtualhome , AI2-THOR~ ai2_thor , and ALFRED~ alfred established interactive 3D environments for household activities, but largely abstracted low-level object manipulation. Recent environments have expanded task diversity, dataset scale, and the realism and interactivity of articulated assets~ behavior1k,robocasa,robocasa365 , enabling increasingly complex and physically grounded household tasks to be studied at scale. summary: Robot manipulation videos provide a rich visual experience, yet recovering robot action and gripper-state annotations from RGB observations still remains challenging. Using the embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point (TCP) pose as the action space, we present TCP4D, a unified model in which a shared 4D scene representation both tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial 2D TCP queries, the tracker directly recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states alongside scene geometry and camera parameters. Introduction sec:intro =-1 Large-scale video data of robot manipulation~ open_x_embodiment_rt_x_2023,agibotworld offer a rich source of experience for learning diverse skills. These data provide an important foundation for modern vision-language-action (VLA) models~ pan2026world,intelligence2025pi05,Falcon and world action models (WAMs)~ dreamzero,fastwam,worldguide,sgwam , whose training relies on action supervision. However, not all videos include synchronized action annotations, and recovering these labels from RGB video alone remains a nontrivial challenge. =-1 Recovering the end effector's motion offers a practical route to obtaining such supervision from videos. This motion can be represented by the tool-center-point (TCP) pose (i.e., ), which specifies the position and orientation of the end effector's tool frame. With a common reference frame, TCP provides a unified action representation: the same pose encodes the same task-space goal across robot platforms, even when their joint configurations differ, since each robot can reach the pose through its own inverse kinematics (IK)~ OnePolicy,unifyrobotactionscamera if within its work range. Recent 4D point tracking methods~ luo2026fourrc,karhade2026any4d,lu2026track4world,sucar2026vdpm4dvideoreconstruction recover scene geometry and track 3D surface points from RGB video. The TCP, however, is the origin of a virtual tool frame and can lie in free space between the gripper fingers. Its image projection can therefore fall on a background pixel. Moreover, point trackers predict only 3D positions not tool orientation, so even an accurate trajectory of the TCP origin does not determine the full TCP pose. Recovering full TCP poses from these trackers therefore relies on additional robot-specific priors and multi-stage post-processing, along which errors accumulate and may lead to inaccurate poses or tracking failures. title: CoBoVLA: Decoupling Language from Action with Discrete Codes for Robust and Interpretable Robot Manipulation

summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve high success rates on the LIBERO benchmark but remain sensitive to paraphrasing. Existing VLAs ranging from 0.6B to 7.5B parameters experience a 22-52 point performance drop on LIBERO-Para while SmolVLA exhibits an even larger decline, from 83\% to 8\%. Because most VLAs jointly learn language understanding and action generation, it is difficult to determine whether a failure originates from misunderstanding an instruction or executing it incorrectly. To address these challenges, we introduce CoBoVLA, or CodeBookVLA, a 250M-parameter VLA that decouples language understanding, planning, and control through learned discrete interpretable codes. A text encoder maps the instructions to shared step codes, which a visual planner then converts into action code sequences executed by a language-independent actor. This design improves robustness to instruction paraphrasing while allowing failures to be traced to individual stages. It also enables efficient real-time control on resource-constrained hardware by encoding instructions only once and using compact discrete representations to keep each component lightweight. CoBoVLA achieves 91.4\% success on LIBERO-Goal, compared with 82.8\% for SmolVLA, under a matched protocol, with 17 ms per control step latency. On LIBERO-Para, it achieves 81.1\% across 4,092 unseen paraphrases and 78.5\% on matched episodes, compared with 36.5\% for SmolVLA LoRA fine-tuned on paraphrases. Without two-step demonstrations, CoBoVLA completes 48.8\% of 160 free-form two-step tasks. Finally, success reaches 91\% when instructions are correctly encoded but falls to 27.2\% otherwise, identifying language understanding as the main source of remaining failures. Together, these results demonstrate that decoupling language understanding and control can improve instruction robustness while making VLA failures easier to diagnose.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera images and a language instruction to robot actions~ pi0,pi05,openvla,smolvla , and on the LIBERO benchmark~ libero the strongest ones now reach 96--98 success~ pi05,openvlaoft,vlaadapter,turbovla . These scores say little about language understanding, since a 0.5M-parameter policy that uses a lookup table of 40 task identifiers in place of language gets 95.8 on LIBERO~ minerva , while paraphrasing the instructions reduces the success of VLAs with 0.6B--7.5B parameters by 22--52 points~ liberopara . We argue that part of this difficulty comes from the architecture. In a VLA, language and control are learned jointly in one network, so the representation of the instruction is mixed with the representation of the motion. This leads to three problems. First, the robustness to rewording has to be learned from robot data, or it has to be added at test time. Second, when the robot fails, the model does not tell us whether it misunderstood the instruction or executed the motion wrongly ( ). Third, the whole network, including its language model, runs at every control step, which makes real-time control difficult on the resource-constrained hardware of a robot. To address these problems, we explore a different design, where understanding and acting communicate only through a discrete interface which can be inspected. The proposed (CodeBook VLA, ) has three stages. A text encoder (stage~1) maps the instruction to a short sequence of discrete step codes, one for each step of the task, and it is trained so that paraphrases of the same instruction are mapped to the same codes ( ). Then, a visual planner takes the current step code together with camera images and robot state, and predicts a chain of action codes, , discrete motion segments which are learned from demonstrations with minimum-description-length (MDL) segmentation ( ). An actor which never sees the language converts the current action codes into motor commands ( ). With this design, paraphrases that are mapped to the same step codes produce the same behavior, because no part after stage~1 sees the words. Also, every failure can be localized to one stage by reading the codes, and the language stage can be improved with text only: all of the paraphrase robustness in this paper comes from training stage~1 on generated paraphrases, without collecting new robot demonstrations. Finally, the architecture is chosen to run in real time on such hardware. The instruction is encoded once, by a 38M-parameter text encoder, instead of by a language model at every control step, and each stage can be small because the discrete interface absorbs its errors: an imprecise output of a small model still selects the right code as long as it lands closer to that code than to any other. Most VLAs fine-tune a pretrained vision-language model to output robot actions, as discrete tokens in OpenVLA~ openvla or through a continuous action head trained with diffusion~ diffusionpolicy or flow matching~ pi0,pi05,openvlaoft,xvla . Several works make them smaller and faster: SmolVLA~ smolvla and VLA-Adapter~ vlaadapter build on backbones of about 0.5B parameters, NanoVLA~ nanovla routes between a small and a large model, and TurboVLA~ turbovla drops the language model from the control path and gets 97.7 on LIBERO with 0.2B parameters. Data augmentation trains the policy on rephrased instructions~ relabel,paraconsensus,synthaug,dial ; on LIBERO-Spatial with their own paraphrases, Li ~ paraconsensus remove nearly all of the paraphrase cost by LoRA fine-tuning of OpenVLA on paraphrases. summary: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly generate future video and robot actions through iterative denoising. Few-step distillation reduces the number of model evaluations, but its coarse updates can move the student away from the teacher's trajectory. We propose Anchored Path Matching (APM), which supervises endpoint and short-transition predictions from states reached by the student. From each state, we continue the teacher to zero noise and use its endpoint and first intermediate state as targets. Modality-routed adapters learn to match both targets from the same starting state. When the two gradients conflict, anchor-priority updates preserve the endpoint gradient and remove the opposing component of the local gradient within each modality. One checkpoint supports 1-, 2-, and 4-step joint generation. The sampling budget can be chosen at deployment without retraining or teacher queries. On RoboTwin 2.0, we train only on Clean demonstrations and evaluate directly on the domain-randomized Random setting. At one step, APM improves closed-loop success over continued base distillation at matched inference budgets by 2.0 percentage points on Clean and 1.4 on Random. Video peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) rises from 30.169 to 32.317 dB, with gains in structural similarity (SSIM) and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS). On two real-robot tasks, APM improves success over the one-step teacher and reduces control-cycle latency by $21.3\times$ relative to the eight-step teacher.Project page: https://jialonglong.github.io/Anchored-Path-Matching/.

However, iterative generation requires repeated model evaluations, leading to substantial inference costs. Few-step distillation addresses this limitation by training a student to approximate a multi-step teacher with fewer sampling steps~ consistency_models,progressive_distillation,anyflow,flash_wam . Supporting multiple sampling budgets with a single student is particularly desirable, as it allows the trade-off between inference efficiency and prediction quality to be adjusted at deployment without retraining. Recent efforts improve few-step WAM distillation through teacher-guided transitions or endpoint supervision. AnyStep-WAM restarts the teacher from the first recycled preview state to supervise subsequent sampling-budget intervals, while its separate endpoint loss is computed from states along the teacher trajectory~ anystep_wam . These approaches provide complementary forms of supervision, but their effectiveness across different sampling budgets remains an important challenge. Specifically, coarse student updates can drive generation away from the teacher trajectory, causing the student to encounter states that the teacher would not normally visit. Consequently, local-transition supervision and endpoint supervision may be applied to different state distributions: a teacher transition provides guidance on local prediction dynamics, whereas an endpoint target constrains the completed video and actions. Supervision based on teacher-trajectory states may therefore be misaligned with the states encountered by the student, while local-transition guidance alone does not directly constrain the final output. Pairing these targets at the same student-reached state could address both limitations, but introduces an additional optimization challenge: their gradients may conflict when updating shared parameters, such that improving local transition matching can undermine endpoint predictions. On two real-robot tasks, single-step APM also outperforms the step-matched undistilled teacher, reducing control-cycle latency from 4323.6 to 203.1 ms relative to the full teacher, a speedup. title: VSpark: Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Our aim is to accelerate autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs), which generate robot actions one token at a time. Speculative decoding makes this possible: a lightweight draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the VLA verifies them in a single pass, accepting only those that match its own predictions, so decoding remains lossless. The speedup, however, is limited in robot control, where many different tokens encode nearly the same motion and a draft close to the correct action is still rejected. To address this, our approach, VSpark, is built upon three design choices: (i) rollouts collected with calibrated action noise, which expose the draft to a wider range of robot states; (ii) feature alignment, which trains the draft to match the VLA's hidden features rather than its output tokens alone; and (iii) continuation reuse, which keeps the predictions the VLA has already computed along rejected drafts as candidates for the next verification step, instead of discarding them. On four VLAs with different action tokenizers and four manipulation benchmarks, VSpark achieves 1.28x to 2.10x speedup while keeping the VLA's decoding lossless.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action models (VLAs) control robots by mapping camera images and a language instruction to actions, building on pretrained vision-language models~ rt-2, openvla . Autoregressive VLAs represent continuous actions as discrete tokens and generate them by the next-token prediction used in pretraining, which lets them inherit the generalization and visual-language understanding of the underlying model~ chen2023pali, driess2023palm, karamcheti2024prismatic . The cost is speed: every action token requires a forward pass of a large model, limiting the control frequency. Progress in action tokenization has reduced this cost but not removed it. Early models assign one token to every action dimension at every timestep~ openvla , whereas recent action tokenizers compress a whole chunk of future actions into a shorter token sequence, so that a single token no longer corresponds to a single action value~ fast,actioncodec,g05 . The remaining tokens are still generated one at a time, and this remains a major bottleneck. The focus of this work is on removing this bottleneck with speculative decoding~ leviathan2023,chen2023 . A lightweight draft model proposes several future tokens, and the VLA being accelerated, the target, verifies them in one parallel pass and accepts the longest prefix that matches its own predictions. Because only matching tokens are accepted, decoding is lossless through exact verification by the target. This property is valuable in robot control: the accelerated policy uses lossless decoding, with no tolerance to tune and exact verification of action tokens. The speedup, however, depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted per verification cycle, which is low for robot actions. Many different tokens encode nearly the same motion, so a draft close to the correct action is still rejected when its tokens differ. Existing speculative decoding methods for VLAs relax verification by accepting drafted tokens that are sufficiently close to the target's predictions~ specvla,kerv,heisd . These acceptance rules rely on per-dimension action bins, where neighboring bins correspond to nearby values of the same action dimension~ rt-2,openvla . This notion of proximity does not directly extend to compressed tokenizers such as FAST~ fast and ActionCodec~ actioncodec , which require the complete token sequence before decoding it into an action chunk. Direct comparison with the target's decoded actions would require the target to generate the remaining tokens of the action chunk before acceptance can be decided. In other words, relaxing acceptance for a single token would require the target to generate the entire remaining action sequence. Token embedding distance offers an alternative that can be evaluated immediately, but we find that it is an unreliable proxy for action distance. Ranking candidate tokens by embedding distance disagrees with ranking them by decoded action distance for about 31 of pairs, and 18 of single-token substitutions in complete FAST sequences do not decode to a valid action at all ( ). When verification is relaxed by embedding distance on -FAST, raising the speedup from to lowers the success rate from 91.7 to 71.4 ( ). This raises our question: can speculative decoding be effective for VLAs with compressed action tokenizers while keeping verification exact? To this end, we introduce VSpark, which keeps verification exact and instead exploits the similarity between actions on the draft side ( ). If many tokens encode nearly the same motion, then the draft should learn from more than token labels, and a rejected token is often nearly right, so what the target predicted after it remains informative. VSpark builds on the parallel drafter DSpark~ dspark and rests on three design choices. First, we train the draft on rollouts collected with calibrated action noise. Drafts are usually trained only on the states visited by the training demonstrations. We adapt noise injection in DART~ dart to draft training by perturbing actions during target rollouts in simulation. DART calibrates noise to discrepancies between a learned policy's actions and those of a supervisor, such as a human expert. We instead use discrepancies between draft and target actions, setting the noise scale to reflect the draft's errors in predicting the target. Second, we introduce feature alignment. Supervision by token labels treats every wrong token alike, however close its action is to the correct one. We therefore feed the target's hidden features to the draft and train it to regress them, giving it a continuous signal that token identity alone does not provide. This raises the average number of tokens committed per verification cycle from 3.22 to 3.87 on -FAST ( ). Third, we propose continuation reuse. When the target verifies a tree of candidates, it also computes what it would predict after each rejected candidate, and standard decoding discards these predictions. We consider draft tokens that match the target's predictions after a rejected token: In VLAs, 45 to 55 of these tokens also match the target's predictions under the corrected prefix ( ). Continuation reuse promotes these predictions into the next draft tree, where they are verified again, ensuring lossless decoding at no extra cost to the target. Acting purely at inference time, continuation reuse requires no training and no change to either model. The outcome of these design choices is that VSpark accelerates four autoregressive VLAs, -FAST, StarVLA-FAST, ActionCodec, and G0.5, which together cover frequency-based and learned vector-quantized action tokenizers. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and SimplerEnv, it achieves to speedup over autoregressive decoding while retaining exact verification of action tokens. Under the same exact verification, VSpark outperforms five recent speculative decoding methods~ eagle3,peagle,dflash,dflash2,dspark on every model and benchmark. This shows that similarity between robot actions can be turned into speed while retaining exact verification. Related Works converts continuous robot actions into discrete tokens that an autoregressive VLA can predict, and maps the generated tokens back into actions. Tokenizers fall into two categories. Per-dimension tokenizers discretize each action dimension into bins: OpenVLA~ openvla predicts seven tokens per control step, three for translation, three for rotation, and one for the gripper. Compressed tokenizers instead encode a chunk of actions jointly across dimensions and timesteps, which shortens the sequence. FAST~ fast applies a discrete cosine transform to the chunk, quantizes the coefficients, and compresses them with byte-pair encoding. ActionCodec~ actioncodec and G0.5~ g05 learn a discrete representation with a neural encoder and vector quantization, using residual quantization to refine the reconstruction. With a compressed tokenizer, a token carries information from several dimensions and timesteps, and the action is recovered only after the whole sequence is decoded. We evaluate VSpark on VLAs with both kinds of compressed tokenizers. accelerates autoregressive generation with lossless decoding by verifying multiple draft tokens in one target pass~ leviathan2023,chen2023 . Tree verification checks several alternative continuations in the same pass~ specinfer,medusa . Developed for large language models, this line of work has concentrated on the draft model, which falls into two categories. Autoregressive drafters run once for every drafted token: EAGLE~ eagle drafts with a single Transformer block that predicts the target's hidden features, EAGLE-2~ eagle2 builds the draft tree dynamically from cumulative draft scores, and EAGLE-3~ eagle3 removes feature regression and trains on draft-generated contexts with multi-layer target features. Parallel drafters instead predict all positions in one pass: P-EAGLE~ peagle and PARD~ pard,pard2 replace the unavailable preceding tokens with learned or mask embeddings, and DFlash~ dflash uses bidirectional attention within a masked block, injecting target features as keys and values in every draft layer. Because such predictions do not depend on the tokens chosen at earlier positions, DSpark~ dspark , DFlash2~ dflash2 , and Domino~ domino add lightweight sequential corrections conditioned on the preceding tokens. Recent work also constructs draft trees from parallel drafters by selecting high-probability branches from the per-position distributions~ ddtree,dominotree,cadtree,chains2trees,zhou2026treespark . Other work reuses target predictions or hidden states that would otherwise be discarded after verification to improve subsequent drafts in large language models~ luo2025turning,koo2026carryover . Speculative decoding has also been extended to vision-language models that generate text~ glance,unilaspec,mmsdsurvey . VSpark builds on DSpark and differs in three respects: it injects calibrated action noise during rollouts, restores the feature supervision that EAGLE-3 removed, and fills the draft tree with target-predicted continuations rather than draft predictions alone. applies this procedure to the action tokens generated by a VLA. Existing methods use the tree decoding of EAGLE-2 and relax the verification rule, accepting a drafted token that differs from the target's prediction when the two are sufficiently close. title: From Perception to Simulation: Unveiling and Empowering Mental Spatial Dynamics in MLLMs
summary: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.

Introduction Spatial reasoning is the ability of an agent to perceive, understand, and mentally manipulate spatial relationships between objects spatialcontext,spatialtree,spatial_survey . It constitutes a fundamental component of how multimodal large language models (MLLMs) understand the physical world. Despite recent advances that enable models to achieve impressive performance on a wide range of visual reasoning tasks mmmu, visualpuzzle, mmr-v , their spatial reasoning capabilities remain limited thinkinspace, spatialladder, spatialtree . This gap has motivated growing interest in systematic investigations of spatial reasoning in MLLMs. Recent work has primarily studied spatial reasoning by focusing on models’ spatial perception capabilities spatial-mllm, embodied-r, sims-v . As illustrated by the first example in Figure fig:intro , these works typically assume static environments, in which the spatial states of objects and agents remain fixed ViewSpatialbench,thinkinspace,mmsibench . Under this setting, models can solve the task by performing a single-pass perception over the input images or videos to localize objects. However, real-world environments are inherently dynamic, where the spatial positions of objects and agents continuously change over time. As shown in the second example of Figure fig:intro , reasoning in such settings requires models to mentally simulate the evolving spatial state of the environment (e.g., the changing direction between the monitor and agent), a capability we refer to as spatial simulation. While existing studies have explored mental simulation, they predominantly focus on isolated objects ominispatial, stare or restricted viewpoints ViewSpatialbench, mindcube , leaving this capability largely underexplored. In cognitive neuroscience, spatial simulation is supported by internal representations like grid cells gridcell1,gridcell2,gridcell3 , which enable humans to mentally track their spatial state without continuous visual feedback. To investigate whether MLLMs exhibit a similar capacity, we introduce MentalGrid, a spatial reasoning benchmark featuring 3,356 question-answer pairs that evaluates models’ ability to predict evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. As illustrated in Figure fig:bench , our benchmark goes beyond static spatial perception by integrating language-guided action sequences into spatial reasoning. It introduces final state prediction and dynamic process tracking tasks, requiring models to predict final spatial states such as distances and directions, as well as to track state changes throughout the movements. Our extensive evaluation of 12 state-of-the-art MLLMs on MentalGrid reveals that existing models struggle with spatial simulation, while the best-performing Gemini-3.1-Pro achieves only around 58 accuracy, remaining approximately 16 behind human performance. Besides, for open-source models, spatial simulation performance is substantially worse than spatial perception. We further analyze the bottlenecks in the model's spatial simulation performance, finding that perceptual limitations constrain performance for simple simulation steps, while inadequate multi-step reasoning becomes the main limitation as complexity increases. To mitigate these limitations, we design a three-stage curriculum learning framework based on 16k curated spatial reasoning samples. This framework starts with foundational perceptual grounding, advances to process-aware simulation training to internalize spatial transitions, and culminates in reinforcement learning-based optimization to refine fine-grained simulation trajectories. This approach yields SpatialWalker, a 3B model that achieves a 33.8 average improvement over its base, surpassing proprietary systems like Gemini-3-Flash. Furthermore, SpatialWalker exhibits robust generalization with 4.9 average performance gains on out-of-domain benchmarks, underscoring the role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence. Our contributions are as follows: (1) MentalGrid Benchmark: a novel benchmark for dynamic spatial simulation that requires tracking evolving states across action sequences without intermediate visual feedback. (2) Curriculum Learning Framework: a three-stage strategy, derived from our diagnostic findings, that evolves from perceptual grounding to spatial simulation trajectory optimization. (3) SpatialWalker Model: a 3B model that outperforms its base by 33.8 , surpasses Gemini-3-Flash, and achieves an average 4.9 out-of-domain gains. title: Plausible Videos Can Lead to Poor Decisions: Diagnosing and CURE-ing World Models for Planning
summary: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly used as world models for planning, yet a world model that makes plausible, realistic-looking videos that are consistent with the training data can produce poor decisions. We address two key questions: (1) when can we trust a world model for planning, and (2) what should we do when we cannot? We introduce CURE (Certify, Upweight, Rollout, Explore), a certificate-guided technique that assesses whether a world model can be trusted for planning and determines what to do next: whether to upweight the training data to debias the model; roll out more samples at test time; or explore by collecting new data where support (how well the training data cover the planner's decisions) is missing. We deploy CURE across multiple domains, spanning simulated physics based on PhyWorld, MuJoCo arm control, and Language-Table pushing in simulation and on real videos. The decisions our certificate trusts have lower regret than those it does not (e.g., 0.06 vs. 0.38 on Language-Table sim and 0.07 vs. 0.38 on MuJoCo contact), whereas video perceptual quality does not identify good decisions. By focusing on decision quality rather than perceptual quality, CURE lowers regret over the best pessimistic decision rule by 10-25% across support levels, and over world-action models, search and policy learning by 41-64%, given the same data.

title: Know When to Zoom: How Small Is Too Small for Vision-Language Models?
comment: Accepted to the SENSE workshop at WACV 2027. 10 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Code, data and a plain-language walkthrough: https://siddvoh.com/know-when-to-zoom/
summary: Online vision-language models often miss small details in large images, because the service shrinks the image, or rejects it, before the model ever sees it. A car 20 pixels wide in an 8000 by 6000 drone photo reaches Claude about 6 pixels wide, and OpenAI's default rejects the photo outright. We measure how much detail survives for seven models from four vendors, using an eye exam of printed codes and 601 questions about small objects in real photos. The smallest text a model reads half the time grows from 6 pixels or less on a small image to a predicted 10 to 13 pixels on a 7680 by 4320 photo at default settings. Zooming wins much of the detail back. Splitting each photo into up to nine tiles raises accuracy by 11.1 to 14.5 percentage points for Claude and Gemini, and by avoiding rejections it lifts GPT-6.1 Sol from 50.7% to 83.7%. A two-step zoom, in which the model first names the region it needs, matches or beats tiles on Gemini and comes within 2.5 points of them on Claude, with about 40% of their image tokens. When a detail is lost, Claude and Gemini both say they cannot tell about half the time, but they fail differently in the rest: Gemini gives a confident wrong answer in 43% to 48% of these cases, Claude in only 5% to 9%. A check based on detail size, run before the call, misses most of the gain from tiles on Claude and Gemini, but Claude's own reply is a reliable trigger: tiling only after an unsure reply comes within 1.4 points of always tiling with 62% to 70% of the image tokens. We turn these findings into five rules for when an agent should zoom, and release the eye exam, every model answer and code at https://siddvoh.com/know-when-to-zoom.

Introduction sec:intro Many questions about images turn on small details. A satellite scene may show a vehicle only a few pixels wide, and a security camera frame may hold a license plate in one corner. Imagine asking a vision-language model about the color of one car in an 8000 by 6000 drone photo of a parking lot, where the car is 20 pixels wide. Claude shrinks the photo to less than a third of its width before the model sees it, so the car arrives about 6 pixels wide. OpenAI, at its default setting, rejects the photo outright. A user who does not know these rules cannot tell whether a wrong answer came from the model or from the shrinking. This happens because every service we tested fits images to its own limits. Newer Claude models shrink a large image to at most 2576 pixels on its long side~ anthropic2026vision , and Gemini turns any image into at most 280 to 2,240 tokens, the small units a model reads, depending on a setting~ google2026mediaresolution . OpenAI's guide says that for GPT-6 Astra the default keeps the full image but rejects very large ones~ openai2026imagesvision , and the two OpenAI models we tested behave the same way. An agent that answers such questions should therefore first ask whether the detail will survive the trip to the model. If it will not, the agent should zoom in, by cropping or tiling the image, before it sends the question. The hard part is knowing when. This paper asks the three questions an agent built on these services must answer to make that decision. How small can a detail be before a service erases it? What does the model say when the detail is gone? And can a simple check before the call say when to zoom? We tested seven models: Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and 3.8 Flash, GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6.1 Sol, and the open model Qwen3.8-27B. From here on we call them Haiku, Sonnet, Flash-Lite, Flash, Luna, Sol and Qwen. For the first question, we gave them an eye exam, much like the letter chart at an optometrist's office. Each test image shows a random five-character code, printed at one of ten text sizes on a plain gray background, the canvas. We call the smallest text size a model reads half the time its readable size. We print the same text sizes on four canvases, from small to large. The larger the canvas, the more a service may shrink it, so comparing the canvases shows how much detail the shrinking removes. For the other two questions, we asked 601 questions about small objects in large photos, taken from three public benchmarks~ wu2024vstar,wang2025divide,zhang2025mmerealworld . We sent each question in up to five ways: as is, at the highest setting, as 4 tiles, as 9 tiles, or as a two-step zoom, in which the model first names the region it needs and then sees that region, cut from the original, next to an overview of the photo. We make three contributions. We give the readable text size for every model and setting we tested, along with the rules each service applies ( , ). For Claude, the documented resize explains much of what the model can read. It fits Haiku closely and Sonnet less well. Gemini sees more than its token count. On real photos, up to nine tiles raise accuracy by 11.1 to 14.5 percentage points for Claude and Gemini, and the two-step zoom matches or beats them on Gemini with about 40 of their image tokens ( ). When a detail is lost, both say they cannot tell about half the time, but Gemini answers the rest with high confidence ( ). We show which signals tell an agent when to zoom. A check on detail size, made before the call, misses most of the gain from tiles on Claude and Gemini, while on Claude, tiling only after an unsure reply nearly matches tiling every photo. We turn these results into five rules, and release the eye exam, every model answer and the code. What the services do to images sec:rules Before asking what models can read, we need to know what each service does to an image ( ). Every service measures an image in tokens. For most, a token is a small square patch of pixels, so a token limit is also a pixel limit. Claude. Claude 4.7 and later models shrink an image until its long side is at most 2576 pixels and it fits in 4,784 tokens, each a square of 28 by 28 pixels~ anthropic2026vision . We call this the native setting. Earlier Claude models used a smaller standard limit of 1568 pixels and 1,568 tokens. Instead of shrinking, the API can also be asked to reject an oversized image with an error~ anthropic2026vision . To see what the native setting gains, we also test Claude at the standard setting, applying its rule ourselves. Gemini. Gemini works differently. Its media resolution setting has four levels, low, medium, high and ultra high, which cap an image at 280, 560, 1,120 and 2,240 tokens~ google2026mediaresolution . Leaving the setting unset, the default, gives the same 1,120 tokens as high. In our measurements, the tokens form a grid shaped like the image: at high, a 4:3 image becomes 38 by 28 tokens, whether it is small or huge. Google does not say how many pixels each token covers, so we estimate it in . In , the 12 MP photo uses the long side we estimate on our 4096 by 3072 canvas, and the 8K photo the one on our 8000 by 6000 canvas. OpenAI. OpenAI's default does not shrink a large image, but it may reject it. Its guide describes patches of 32~by~32 pixels, and says an image is rejected if it still needs more than 30,000 patches after any resizing~ openai2026imagesvision . The guide does not cover Luna or Sol, so we measured their rules ourselves. At the default auto setting, both keep the image at full size. The service rejected exactly the images that need more than 30,000 patches. A 7680 by 4320 photo needs 32,400, so the default rejects it. A rejected image returns an error message, and the model never answers. The high setting instead shrinks any larger image to at most 2,500 patches. Both settings count 1.2 tokens per patch. Qwen. For the open model Qwen, the service that hosts it follows the model's released image processor~ qwen2026qwen38_27b , which shrinks an image only when it needs more than 16,384 tokens, each 32 by 32 pixels. So Qwen sees far more pixels than Claude, Gemini, or OpenAI's high setting. We checked all these rules against the token counts the services reported. After allowing for the tokens of our fixed text prompt, the counts these rules predict matched the reported ones for every eye-exam image the services accepted. Gemini's image tokens also matched in all 6,447 photo calls that got an answer. An agent can therefore estimate, before the call, how many pixels a detail will keep. What it still needs to know is how many pixels the model needs, and that is what the eye exam measures. Study design sec:design Models. We compared the vendors at two matched tiers. The small tier has Haiku~ anthropic2026haiku55 , Flash-Lite~ google2026gemini35flashlite and Luna~ openai2026gpt6astra . The mid tier has Sonnet~ anthropic2026sonnet55 , Flash~ google2026gemini38flash and Sol~ openai2026gpt61sol . The open model Qwen serves as a reference~ qwen2026qwen38_27b . Every model got the same prompt, the same image files and the same answer format. Each ran at a low reasoning level with an output limit of 8,192 tokens. We asked once more when we could not read a reply. Our release holds every prompt and setting, and the model version each service reported. Eye exam. Printed codes make a clean test, because a read is either exactly right or not. Each test image shows a random five-character code in black on a small white label ( ). The characters come from 22 letters and digits, leaving out look-alikes such as O and 0. A guess is right only one time in 22 per character, so a lucky full read is very rare. A thick red ring around the label stays visible after any shrinking, so the hard part is reading it, not finding it. We measure text size as the cap height, the height of a capital letter in pixels, at ten sizes from 4 to 128. The canvases are plain gray, at 1024 by 768, 2048 by 1536, 4096 by 3072 and 8000 by 6000 pixels, and we name each by its long side. Each canvas and size has 20 codes, so each setting sees 800 images. We sent a fixed 10 of the images a second time, and 84 to 100 of the repeated reads gave the same code. Real photos. Real questions ask about objects in whole scenes, not about a marked label. We took 601 multiple-choice questions about small details in large photos, from three benchmarks. From HR-Bench 8K we drew 150 questions, 75 from each of its two tasks~ wang2025divide . summary: Closed-loop vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely continuously on multi-view cameras, yet existing visual attacks typically hijack sensor streams with 2D patches or alter target object meshes that require retraining when manipulation objects change. We introduce RefCloth, a framework that optimizes one persistent adversarial tablecloth on a frozen source policy and deploys it zero-shot across unseen tasks and target models without modifying task objects or cameras. Throughout manipulation, static third-person and moving wrist views observe this shared world-bound texture under evolving occlusions. To generalize across shifting surface views while bridging the gap between differentiable and native renderers, RefCloth combines bounded texture parameterization with shared surface UV transformations and a same-path clean reference that removes static rendering offsets at initialization. Across four LIBERO suites in native simulation, one frozen texture transfers from OpenVLA-OFT to $π_0$ and $π_{0.5}$, reducing success relative to an unoptimized cloth by 62.50 and 43.75 percentage points on average and far exceeding amplitude- and variation-matched random controls. Dual-view audits and target closed-loop camera interventions show that moving wrist exposure drives over twice the standalone drop of the main view with strong synergy, while ablations confirm the roles of UV diversification and path calibration.

This reliance exposes VLA policies to visual attacks via image patches~ roboticattack,upa,edpa,tapdreamer , object textures~ tex3d,unitexture , and scene perturbations~ trap . Yet the practical threat of an attack hinges on two questions, how much modification privilege the attacker needs, and whether one perturbation transfers across tasks, objects, and models without retraining. Existing attack carriers struggle to satisfy both criteria. Camera-coordinate patches~ patch,upa,edpa require privileged access to hijack live sensor streams, whereas object-bound textures~ meshadv,tex3d,unitexture and CoT surfaces~ trap must alter target meshes or retrain for new objects, tasks, or policies while occupying minimal pixel area ( a). Instead, we investigate a passive workspace tablecloth that requires neither sensor intrusion nor object modification, remaining fixed and reusable without retraining across tasks and policies. Simultaneously, routing the unperturbed base cloth through the identical synthesis path eliminates the static zero-point renderer offset at initialization, substantially improving zero-shot transfer across target policies over an uncalibrated native reference ( c). One exported PNG is then deployed frozen across unseen tasks and target models. title: You Only Encode Once: Sub-Pixel-Shifted Frames for Arbitrary-Scale Remote Sensing Super-Resolution with 2D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Arbitrary-scale super-resolution (ASSR) of remote sensing images remains challenging due to the limited high-frequency information in a single low-resolution (LR) observation. While multi-frame SR can exploit complementary sub-pixel information, existing approaches often require real multi-frame training sequences and repeated feature encoding, increasing data acquisition demands and computational costs. To address these limitations, we propose SPS-GS (Sub-Pixel-Shifted Gaussian Splatting), an encode-once framework that learns from multi-phase LR observations synthesized from individual high-resolution images, without requiring real multi-frame training sequences. Specifically, Phase-Coherent Aliasing Demodulation (PCAD) exploits shift-dependent aliasing through Fourier-based alignment, phase-aware residual fusion, and least-squares aliasing estimation, enabling multi-frame information to be integrated before a single deep encoding pass. Gaussian Projection Alignment (GPA) then iteratively refines Gaussian centers and colors using multi-observation back-projection to promote observation consistency. The refined Gaussians support continuous rendering at arbitrary scales. Extensive experiments on five remote sensing datasets demonstrate strong reconstruction performance against single-image and multi-frame SR baselines, while maintaining competitive inference efficiency at common scales. The code will be publicly released.

title: Learning Agent-Centric Vision-Language-Action World Models for Autonomous Driving
summary: Recent progress in integrating vision-language-action (VLA) models with world modeling has significantly advanced end-to-end autonomous driving by allowing systems to reason about imagined futures instead of merely reacting to current observations. However, most world VLA models generate future frames at the pixel level with plenty of dense visual tokens. Although such generated futures can be visually plausible, they preserve many driving-irrelevant appearance details, i.e., only a small portion of the tokens directly encode critical planning-relevant factors, such as agent geometry, motion dynamics, and interactions. This introduces a significant performance bottleneck. An important question thus arises: what world state should a world VLA model reason over to support planning beyond pixel-level prediction? We argue that planning-oriented world modeling should focus on a compact and structured agent-centric latent state that captures the interactions between objects in the driving scene over time. As such, we introduce AgentWorld, an agent-centric VLA world model that uses discrete agent tokens jointly for reasoning and trajectory planning. Each token is dynamically grounded to a surrounding agent associated with its object's state, such as semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context. AgentWorld learns these tokens through three key processes: explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop experiments under diverse driving scenarios show that AgentWorld enhances planning capabilities, fully exploits visual evidence and agent dynamics, and yields interpretable agent-centric world states.

VLA models inherit the instruction-following and reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs)~ achiam2023gpt4, bai2023qwenvl, bai2025qwen25vl, alayrac2022flamingo, liu2024llava, liu2024improved, ren2026grounding , effectively connecting perception, reasoning, and action generation within a unified framework. World models complement this ability by predicting how the driving scene will evolve before an action is taken. Recent efforts aim to integrate these two approaches into VLA world models~ wang2026learning, lu2025uniugp, cen2025worldvla, liu2026driveworld, zeng2025futuresightdrive , enabling VLA systems to consider imagined futures to produce more reasonable actions. Despite this promising paradigm shown in Fig.~ fig:paradigm , most prior VLA world models imagine the future frames through pixel-level generation with autoregressive or multi-step diffusion. Although such generated future frames can be visually plausible, they retain numerous task-irrelevant visual details, i.e., texture, lighting, background, and visual continuity. Only a small portion of tokens explicitly encode r 0.46 Visual grounding results (UniAD metric) and token efficiency of VLA models. fig:token planning-relevant cues, including agent geometry, motion dynamics, and interactive behaviors. This introduces a significant bottleneck in VLA world models. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:token , existing VLA world models demand far more tokens than the fine-tuned base model, i.e., Qwen2-VL~ wang2024qwen2vl , yet bring only slight planning improvement. Moreover, the visual grounding ablation reveals that removing image cues only slightly degrades existing world VLA models, even with their heavy use of dense visual tokens. This suggests that the visual inputs in these models are not yet fully transformed into planning-relevant reasoning, with many of the visual tokens instead being used for image generation. As such, the core challenge is not simply how to generate visually plausible future frames, but how to integrate world modeling with VLA through a compact, structured, and task-aligned state. An important question thus arises: what world state should a VLA world model reason over to support planning beyond pixel-level prediction? Motivated by JEPA-style paradigms~ lecun2022path, assran2023self, maes2026leworldmodel , which prioritize predictive abstraction over pixel reconstruction, we argue that planning-oriented world modeling should emphasize a latent world state that captures the temporal interactions among objects in driving scenes. Rather than focusing on reconstructing dense visual futures, this state abstracts the scene into decision-relevant entities and their evolving relationships. We implement this idea by breaking down the scene into temporally evolving agents, each defined by semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion state, and interaction context. This structured abstraction enables the policy to recognize relevant agents, predict their motion evolution, and reason about how their future behaviors will influence the ego’s trajectory. In this way, we align the latent world state with the causal structure of driving, shifting world modeling from future frame generation to structured reasoning about interacting agents. In this paper, we introduce AgentWorld, an agent-based world VLA model designed for fully autonomous driving, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:paradigm . AgentWorld integrates causal reasoning, predictive world modeling, and agent interactions into a cohesive framework. In AgentWorld, the driving environment is represented by a set of discrete agent tokens, labeled as <agent i>. These tokens are utilized for both reasoning and trajectory planning. This structure creates a well-defined interface among perception, reasoning, and planning processes. To make these latent agents physically meaningful, AgentWorld anchors them to 4D geometric features and 2D visual cues, and updates their hidden states through the MLLM into contextual representations of semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction. AgentWorld learns these tokens via explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and agent-oriented reinforcement learning (RL) with group relative policy optimization~ guo2025deepseek . The resulting agent tokens deliver a compact, physically grounded, and interaction-aware representation of the world state, facilitating interpretable reasoning and planning regarding surrounding agents in driving scenarios. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of AgentWorld across diverse driving scenarios. By reasoning over interpretable agent-centric latent states, AgentWorld improves planning performance and better leverages visual evidence. These results validate agent-centric world states as an effective intermediate representation for VLA-based autonomous driving. We introduce an agent-centric latent state for planning-oriented world modeling, which represents the driving scene as temporally evolving agents grounded in 3D geometry, motion, semantics, and interaction context. We propose AgentWorld, an agent-centric world VLA model that instantiates this state with discrete agent tokens. Experiments on open-loop and closed-loop benchmarks show consistently improved planning performance and more interpretable world states. title: ReTouchGS: Ultralight Render-free Aesthetic Color Enhancement and Transfer for 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic scene reconstruction. Existing 3DGS color transfer and interactive editing methods are guided by reference images and user-specified color adjustments. However, in many applications, users simply want aesthetically guided color enhancement that automatically makes the scene more visually appealing while maintaining consistent colors and tones across viewpoints. We present ReTouchGS, to our knowledge the first framework for reference-free aesthetic color enhancement of pretrained 3DGS models. It predicts a scene-level color lookup table (LUT) from the model and its associated camera parameters. ReTouchGS also supports reference-guided color transfer by fitting a scene-level LUT using one edited view of the same scene and its corresponding original render. A shared blend-aware color refinement network with only 44.7K parameters refines an analytic color update to realize either color mapping without rendering. It preserves geometry and delivers standard 3DGS assets in seconds. We also design the ReTouch3D benchmark to support the evaluation of aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer across viewpoints. Experiments demonstrate high color accuracy and strong generalization to unseen scenes in both aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer.

Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl3Dgaussians enables photorealistic reconstruction and real-time rendering of reusable scene assets. As these assets support immersive viewing and visual creation, their aesthetic appeal becomes increasingly important. Adjusting a scene's exposure, color balance, and tone can improve its overall aesthetic presentation. Therefore, creators need tools that automatically enhance scene colors or transfer preferred colors and tones from an edited view, with consistent results across viewpoints ( ). In 2D photography, learning from expert retouching provides a foundation for automatic aesthetic enhancement. Datasets such as MIT-Adobe FiveK~ bychkovsky2011fivek and PPR10K~ liang2021ppr10k pair photographs with expert edits, making photographic aesthetic preferences available for learning. Image enhancement methods learn these preferences through image-adaptive lookup tables (LUTs)~ zeng2020learning,yang2022adaint,yang2022seplut and color-aware tone curves~ serrano2024namedcurves , adjusting color and tone based on image content to improve aesthetic presentation. Users may also want to bring these aesthetic enhancements to 3D scenes. Several studies support 3D appearance editing guided by reference images or user input. Reference-guided color transfer~ wang2024bilarf,xiao2025multiview propagates adjustments from a retouched view, and interactive editing~ reparamgs provides palette and luminance controls. Similarly, reference-based stylization~ fpgs,zhuang2025styleme3d transfers a chosen visual style. However, users often seek a more visually appealing scene without having a reference image or a specific set of color adjustments in mind. Meeting this need requires automatic, reference-free aesthetic color enhancement of pretrained 3DGS assets, a task that existing work has not addressed. Extending aesthetic enhancement to 3DGS presents three challenges. First, image-adaptive enhancement applied independently to each view can produce different colors and tones~ xiao2025multiview , requiring a consistent retouching decision for the whole scene. Second, preserving the retouched appearance in the model for subsequent novel-view rendering requires faithfully encoding this decision in Gaussian color parameters. However, the order of nonlinear color transformation and Gaussian blending affects the resulting pixel colors, so directly transforming each Gaussian's color produces discrepancies with the target pixel colors. Third, rendering-based editing~ wang2024bilarf,saad repeatedly renders the scene during per-scene optimization, adding substantial computation even for color adjustments. Such optimization must also preserve the reconstructed geometry and view-dependent appearance to avoid structural or appearance artifacts. These requirements motivate render-free color updates that preserve geometry and opacity. In this paper, we propose , to our knowledge the first framework for reference-free aesthetic color enhancement of pretrained 3DGS assets, and it also supports reference-guided color transfer. For reference-free enhancement, an aesthetic enhancement network learns from an image enhancer trained on expert-retouched photographs and predicts a scene-level LUT from the asset and its associated camera parameters. The resulting RGB-to-RGB mapping is shared across viewpoints of the 3DGS scene. For color transfer, we instead fit this mapping to a user-edited view and its corresponding original render. Both tasks use a shared render-free color update stage that combines an analytic color update with learned color corrections from the blend-aware color refinement network, preserving geometry and opacity in a standard 3DGS asset. The framework uses only 180.2K network parameters for reference-free enhancement and 44.7K for color transfer. We also introduce the benchmark with scene-consistent color targets for 37 scenes. delivers retouched assets in seconds and achieves mean color errors of 5.50 for aesthetic enhancement and 4.03 for reference-guided color transfer on views beyond the capture trajectory. It outperforms all baselines in color accuracy, PSNR, and LPIPS on both tasks. We develop a shared blend-aware color refinement network that refines analytic color updates to embed predicted or reference-fitted color mappings in standard Gaussian assets without rendering. Experiments show that outperforms all evaluated baselines in color accuracy, PSNR, and LPIPS on both tasks. title: Event-Based Person Detection for Maritime UAV Search
comment: Accepted at the 5th Workshop on Maritime Computer Vision (MaCVi), WACV 2027
summary: Maritime search and rescue requires locating people in the water quickly, motivating the use of UAVs to survey the search area. During flight, camera motion and the longer exposures used in low light can blur small targets and hinder person detection. Event cameras record brightness changes as they occur, reducing the motion blur associated with longer exposure times. We investigate their use for maritime person detection by generating synthetic events using the v2e event simulator from public MOBDrone rescue videos and retaining the existing annotations. We compare the recurrent vision transformer model RVT-T with YOLOv8n and RT-DETR-R18 trained on exposure-matched images. On 843 test samples from held-out recordings, RVT-T achieves 15.63% person AP50:95, compared with 6.89% for YOLOv8n and 9.44% for RT-DETR-R18 under 100 ms synthetic exposure. Increasing exposure times from 50 to 200 ms progressively reduces frame-based detection accuracy, widening the gap to the event model. To evaluate the feasibility of on-board processing, we deploy our detector on a Jetson Orin Nano platform. The RVT-T model retains its accuracy and requires approximately 136 ms and 2.02 J per sample, allowing real-time processing on the UAV.
