Introduction Maritime search and rescue brings together the urgency of locating a person in distress and the difficulty of searching a large expanse of water. Camera-equipped UAVs can support this task by providing an aerial view and helping rescue teams locate people who have fallen overboard~ mobdrone . Their usefulness depends on both how quickly they can survey the search area and how reliably a person can be recognized in the captured observations. Faster flight could shorten the time needed to cover a search area, making reliable detection during motion an important capability for aerial rescue systems. Maintaining reliable detection is difficult when people occupy only a few pixels against the water background. Low illumination and rapid camera motion further challenge conventional imaging. In low light, increasing exposure time collects more light, but also allows motion to spread a target's appearance over more of the image, resulting in a blurred image~ nighttimeevents . At a given exposure time, faster image motion likewise increases blur. These effects connect the practical goals of searching in low light and flying faster to a common visual problem: preserving enough target detail for person detection. Event cameras offer an alternative way to capture this detail. Instead of accumulating a complete image over an exposure, they report brightness changes at individual pixels together with their timestamps~ eventsurvey . Their high temporal resolution reduces motion blur, while their wide dynamic range supports imaging across large brightness variations~ eventsurvey . Research on nighttime event imaging also demonstrates their potential for capturing motion in low-light scenes~ nighttimeevents . For maritime search, these properties motivate an event-based view of the visibility challenges faced by aerial cameras, with the prospect of supporting faster search and operation under difficult illumination. For onboard use, detection performance must be considered alongside computing and power requirements. Prior maritime vision studies have examined how detector compression and hardware adaptation trade accuracy for inference efficiency~ rizk2022marineedge,heller2022marineedge . Bringing event-based vision into this setting calls for a corresponding understanding of its detection performance and embedded processing cost. Evaluating both connects the promise of a different sensing approach to the hardware available on a search UAV. In this work, we explore event-based vision as a sensing approach for person detection in maritime UAV search. Public MOBDrone rescue footage and its existing annotations provide a common basis for evaluating event-based and frame-based person detection~ mobdrone . Using simulated events derived from this footage, we study detection under exposure blur (Fig.~ fig:teaser ) and assess the onboard processing requirements through measurements on an Orin Nano. The study connects an application-level motivation for event cameras with detection evidence and practical deployment considerations. Our contributions are as follows: We establish a reproducible MOBDrone-derived evaluation protocol that pairs simulated events and exposure-integrated images while preserving source separation and annotation times. We characterize the person-detection benefit of an event-based system under synthetic exposure blur, including its sensitivity to exposure duration and its associated false positives. We measure the trained detectors' accuracy, latency, and energy consumption on a Jetson Orin Nano to characterize the tradeoff between person-detection performance and onboard processing cost. Related Work Event-based vision Event-based vision offers an alternative way to observe moving objects under challenging imaging conditions. An event camera records brightness changes independently at each pixel, reporting their timing rather than collecting a complete image over a shared exposure~ eventsurvey . Its high temporal resolution helps preserve motion detail, while its wide dynamic range accommodates large differences in scene brightness~ eventsurvey . These properties are relevant to maritime monitoring from moving UAVs, where small targets must be distinguished against water backgrounds with changing illumination and reflections. Simulators make event data available for exploring such applications using rendered scenes or existing videos, partially compensating for the limited availability of annotated event data. ESIM generates events through adaptive scene rendering~ esim , while video-to-event methods allow annotated video datasets to be reused for event-based learning~ videotoevents . The v2e toolbox converts video frames into events with models of sensor response and noise~ v2e . This provides a practical route for maritime researchers to build on existing footage and object annotations. Studies of synthetic-to-real learning further demonstrate transfer to real events for object recognition and semantic segmentation~ videotoevents , with DA4Event improving transfer for recognition through domain adaptation~ da4event . Event-based object detection has already produced successful examples in automotive perception. The Gen1 and 1 Megapixel (1Mpx) benchmarks provide large-scale recordings with annotations for road users, supporting the development and comparison of learned detectors~ gen1,red . The Recurrent Event-camera Detector (RED) uses memory to combine information over time and achieves detection performance comparable to frame-based models on 1Mpx~ red . Recurrent Vision Transformers (RVT) combine spatial attention with temporal memory to improve the balance between detection accuracy and processing time~ rvt . Later work addresses practical requirements: SAST reduces computation by selecting informative regions, while LEOD makes better use of limited annotations through self-training~ sast,leod . Together, these data-generation tools and established detectors provide a starting point for bringing event-based vision to maritime monitoring. We build on v2e and the Tiny variant of RVT (RVT-T)~ rvt to investigate person detection in aerial rescue footage and its embedded processing requirements. Maritime object detection Public aerial datasets support the development of visual detection for maritime search and rescue. MOBDrone provides drone footage with annotations for people in the water and other maritime objects~ mobdrone . On SeaDronesSee~ seadronessee , YOLOv7-Sea adapts a frame-based detector to maritime UAV imagery through an additional small-object prediction head and an attention module~ yolov7sea . LCSC-UAVNet likewise studies lightweight small-object detection from a maritime UAV perspective~ lcscuavnet . These studies connect detector design to the target scales and image content encountered in aerial maritime observation. Event-based perception has also been explored for marine objects. Aelmore et al.~ aelmore combine event filtering, clustering, and motion analysis for vessel detection and tracking. Marine Event Vision uses event-based generalized Hough-transform template matching and clustering to detect objects on the water surface and underwater~ marineeventvision . These applications motivate further exploration of event sensing for maritime vision. Our study focuses on aerial person detection and examines how exposure blur affects the comparison between event-based and frame-based systems. Embedded maritime vision Embedded evaluations connect maritime perception algorithms to the computing resources available on their platforms. Heller et al.~ heller2022marineedge study YOLO-based marine object detection and its optimization for several edge devices. Rizk et al.~ rizk2022marineedge examine pruning and quantization for human detection in marine environments. For fluvial navigation, Lambert et al.~ lambert2023deployability compare segmentation networks and evaluate their performance on a Jetson Nano, relating scene understanding to inference speed on embedded hardware. Together, these studies motivate evaluating visual accuracy alongside actual device performance. We apply this perspective to event-based aerial person detection by measuring the trained models' accuracy, latency, and energy on an Orin Nano. Methodology Event Data An event stream is a sequence of brightness-change measurements, each represented as ~ eventsurvey . The coordinates locate the responding pixel, records the time of the change, and the polarity indicates whether brightness increased or decreased. Each pixel triggers an event when its log intensity changes by a contrast threshold relative to its stored reference~ eventsurvey . The reference is updated after each event, allowing the pixel to report subsequent changes independently. Positive (ON) and negative (OFF) events describe increases and decreases in brightness, respectively. As a person's boundary moves across the image, successive pixels respond to the contrast between the person and the surrounding water. UAV motion can produce this response even for a stationary target, while waves and changing reflections generate additional events in the background. Together, these measurements describe where and when changes occur as the camera and objects move. Our red-and-blue event views accumulate these measurements over a short time window: red indicates positive events, blue indicates negative events, and white indicates no events; dark pixels indicate overlapping positive and negative activity. To use this information for detection, we collect events over a recent time interval and organize them into spatial maps of event counts, separated by time and polarity. Dataset We use MOBDrone because it provides continuous aerial rescue footage and existing object annotations, supporting both video-to-event conversion and exposure formation from the same scenes~ mobdrone . The dataset contains 66 video fragments with a native resolution of . We retain all five annotated categories: person, boat, surfboard, wood, and lifebuoy, with person detection as the primary application task. The person category includes people in the water and on boats or boards. To evaluate generalization across recordings, we assign original video identities to disjoint training, validation, and test sets, keeping all fragments and observation variants from each source together. We define a sample as one annotated time together with its corresponding frame observation or event history and object labels.
